edits.chapter_key: skins, blood, and waiting periods
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the purity of skins, bones, hair, and wool. What follows is drawn from the book of questions and answers mentioned earlier, which its compiler arranged in the order of the chapters of the book دَعَائِمُ الْإِسْلَامِ.

Question: What do you say, O ray of the sun of guidance, concerning impure garments — or the skins of carrion, or the skins of beasts of prey — when they cling to the body while either the skin or the body is wet? Must the body be washed, or not? The same question applies to garments washed by the hands of polytheists.

Answer: If any such thing clings to the body, the body must be washed. The same ruling applies to whatever polytheists have washed with their hands.

Question: What do you say concerning what has come in تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ — that the goat is not shorn of its hair as the sheep is shorn of its wool, that benefit may be taken from it while the animals are alive, and that it is lawful to be clothed in it and to pray in it and upon it? The passage further states that the rest of the animal is lawful — its flesh, its skins, and its bones — and that these are purified if the animal is properly slaughtered. Given all this, our master, may one pray upon the goat's hair and skins if they were taken after the slaughter?

Answer: If the goat's hair and skins are taken after it has been properly slaughtered, prayer upon them is permitted. The goat is a kind of sheep: its private parts are uncovered, its tail turns upward, and it has two horns. It is most common in India.

Question: Concerning a lawful animal — when some of its wool, fleece, or hair is shorn from it while it is still alive: must that shorn material be washed as an impure garment is washed, or not? And if there is moisture in it before it is washed, and it touches a garment or the body, does it render them impure, or not?

Answer: The text states that prayer is not permitted in it until it has been washed, yet the material itself is not impure.

Question: What does our master say — may God perpetuate his guidance — concerning a vessel made from the skins of carrion in the district of Waghar, which is a large town whose people are mostly unbelievers? The vessel is filled with ghee or oil and brought to Ahmedabad, and what is in it is then sold. Is that permitted or not? And if soap is made from it, mixed with lye and soda ash, is the sale and purchase of that soap permitted or not?

Answer: If anything edible is placed in this vessel, it becomes impure, and one may not pray in a garment that such a thing has touched. The sale and purchase of the ghee or the soap are permitted, but the buyer must be informed that they are impure. It is not lawful, however, to sell or to buy the skins of carrion themselves.

And from the book تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ:

> ولا يجز الشعر من المعز الا بعد الذبح فان جز وهو حيّ فهو ميّة

The hair of the goat is not to be shorn except after slaughter. If it is shorn while the animal is alive, it counts as carrion. This ruling applies to the goat in particular. And from the same book: the goat is not shorn of its hair as the sheep is shorn of its wool, so that benefit may be taken from it while the animals are alive, and it is lawful to be clothed in it and to pray in it and upon it. The rest of the animal is likewise lawful — its hair, its skins, its bones, and whatever else belongs to it — and these are purified if the animal is properly slaughtered.

And from مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ: if a person's bone is broken, it is not permitted to patch it except with the bone of an animal whose flesh is eaten and which has been properly slaughtered. Whoever patches one of his bones with the bone of carrion, or with the bone of an animal whose flesh is not eaten, or with the bone of a dead human being, must remove it and repeat every prayer he has prayed. The ruling authority compels him to do so if his case becomes known. If it is not known until he dies and he himself did not know of it, it is not removed after his death. And one may not take benefit from the hair of human beings as one takes benefit from the hair of beasts.

And from تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ, on the view that benefit may be taken from a covering made of carrion that does not adhere: the meaning is that it does not cling to anything pure while either of the two is wet, so that impurity reaches it. And from كِتَابُ الْأَخْبَارِ:

> وَكَرِهُوا أَنْ يُنْتَفَعَ بِلَحْمِ الْخِنْزِيرِ

And they held it reprehensible to take benefit from the flesh of swine.

I come now to menstruation and postpartum bleeding, drawing again upon that same book of questions and answers.

Question: What do you say concerning what has come in the Sharia — that the menstruating woman wraps herself with a wrapper from below the navel to the knees, and that her husband may have of her what is above the wrapper and what is below it? So, our master, may he touch her whole body short of intercourse? Answer: Yes, he may touch her body, but it is better that he avoid what is beneath the wrapper, for fear that the fluid reach her womb.

Another matter: if a woman menstruates and remains in that state for ten days, and after those ten days the blood continues for two, three, four, or five more days, she does not pray and does not fast, her husband does not approach her, and she does not make up the prayers after her purification, provided she is certain that menstrual blood is distinguishable from the blood of istihadah. If she is in doubt about the blood, then she is a mustahadah.

Another matter: whoever misses the prayer of the Feast of Ghadir and its fast makes them up after that day, on whatever day it may be, performing the make-up at the time of the sun's decline, just as it would have been.

Question: What do you say concerning a woman who becomes pure from menstruation or from postpartum bleeding within the time of a prayer, and when she has finished the washing, the time of the prayer has passed? Is she obliged to make up that prayer or not? Answer: If she was leisurely, she makes it up; but if she was diligent in her washing and did not finish it until the time passed, she is not obliged to make up that prayer.

And from the answers of our master al-Numan, may God sanctify his soul, to the governor of Zawatah, Khattab ibn Wasim: You asked me about a blind woman, and how she is to manage her menstruation. Command her to insert a piece of cotton or a white cloth, and to have it inspected by a woman whose religion she trusts. As long as the blood comes out upon it she is menstruating; and when it comes out white she has become pure, so she washes, prays, and fasts, and her husband comes to her. She does likewise at the beginning of her menstruation if she does not perceive it herself.

Another matter: if a woman becomes pure from menstrual blood in the month of Ramadan before sunset and fears harm from washing, it is permitted to her to perform tayammum and to fast, and she does not make up that fast. Likewise the man who has a nocturnal emission in the month of Ramadan: if he fears illness for himself from washing at night, he performs tayammum and fasts, and he does not make up that fast.

Question: Concerning the woman who becomes pure in the month of Ramadan from menstruation and fasts nine days, and menstruation comes to her on the tenth day — is her fasting of those nine days established or not? Answer: It has been mentioned that the least of menstruation is three days, and the least of purity is ten days.

Question: From the book of purification, that the most of the days of menstruation is ten days: if the bleeding exceeds this term, are her prayer and her fasting established, even if the blood is thick and foul, or not? Answer: Menstrual blood and the blood of istihadah have both been described, and the distinction between them made, so rely upon the text in that matter.

Question: It has come in the Sharia that the limit of postpartum bleeding is forty days, and in some books sixty days. Which of the two, our master, is more correct? Answer: This answer is from our master Hasan ibn Nuh in his own words, may God sanctify his soul. He said: the woman in her postpartum period reckons the nifas according to the duration to which she is accustomed, and the blood of nifas is distinguishable from the blood of istihadah. Whenever she becomes pure and is clean of blood, she washes, prays, and fasts, and her husband comes to her. And it is said in the book of purification: the woman in her postpartum period, when she has given birth, or has seen blood before delivery in a state of menstruation, continues with the blood until it ceases from her; and the menstruating woman washes when she becomes pure. If the blood is prolonged with her, she is a mustahadah, and the blood of nifas is distinguishable from the blood of istihadah, just as we mentioned the distinction of menstrual blood from the blood of istihadah. And it is said in مُخْتَصَرُ الْآثَارِ: the woman in her postpartum period is like the menstruating woman, and in a state like hers; what is obligatory upon her and upon her husband in her affair is what is obligatory in menstruation, and she washes when the blood of nifas ceases from her. And it is said in مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ: the woman in her postpartum period leaves the prayer for the number of the days of her nifas and according to what her custom has been, if she has a custom; and likewise in دَعَائِمُ الْإِسْلَامِ, which sets her upon this same course.

I myself saw, in one of the books of the Sharia of the people of the House (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), the term of the woman in her postpartum period reckoned by days. It is mentioned there that the least of nifas is twenty days, the middle is forty days, and the most is sixty days; and that this is when the blood continues with her, so that it does not exceed sixty days; and that menstrual blood is other than the blood of istihadah; and that it never falls short of twenty days, and the woman in her postpartum period does not become pure before twenty days. This is the sense of the words of that book. As for its exact wording, I did not find it at the time of writing this page; if I live and come upon that book, I will set down its wording exactly, God willing.

As for the point intended, I have made clear to you that the woman in her postpartum period, when she is clean of blood, has become pure after twenty days. This is the ruling concerning her, decisively. Thereafter she relies upon what she is accustomed to. If the blood exceeds her custom, she looks to see whether the blood has changed or is as it was. If it has changed, then it is the blood of istihadah; and if it has not changed, then its ruling is as I described at first. And our master al-Numan, may God sanctify his soul, mentioned in اَلْمُنْتَخَبَةُ:

> وَالنُّفَسَاءُ تَجْلِسُ قَدْرَ الْحَيْضِ
> فَاِنْ تَمَادَى دَمُهَا بِالْفَيْضِ
> تَرَيَّصْتُ لِمَبْلَغِ الشَّهْرَیْنِ
> ثُمَّ قَضَتْ مَا بَيْنَمَا الْوَقْتَيْنِ
> تَطَهَّرَتْ حِيَاطَةُ لِتُسْلِمَ
> مِنَ الصَّلَاةِ وَالصِّيَامِ بَعْدَ مَا
> إِنِ اسْتَحَاضَتْ بَعْدَ هَذَا الْاِنْقِضَا
> وَقَدْ ذَكَرْتُ حُكْمَهَا فِي مَا مَضَى

This applies when the postpartum blood extends beyond a woman's established pattern, and the blood is turbid, thick, and foul — the character of true nifas blood. In that case, she refrains from prayer and fasting and keeps away from her husband until two full months have elapsed. If the blood continues beyond the two months, she is unquestionably a mustahadah. She then washes and makes up the prayers and fasts she abandoned — from the completion of her customary term to the completion of the two months — by way of precaution, since this is a matter of doubt: it is possible that menstruation followed the nifas. That is the ruling of nifas, and God and His Messenger know best. With this, the answer of our master is complete, by the praise and bounty of God.

It is said in the book مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ: if she begins the prayer at its proper time and then menstruates, she need not make up that prayer. If she menstruates for a day or two and the blood then stops, and she observes ten days of purity, that does not count as menstruation — for menstruation is not less than three days — and if she abandoned the prayer during that time, she repeats it. If she sees blood for a day or two, then sees purity for fewer than ten days, then sees blood again, the first and second episodes together constitute menstruation.

It is said in تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ that the word nifas was mentioned only in connection with childbirth, and that what is meant by it is the blood that accompanies it. This is made plain by what was reported from the Messenger of God, who said to one of his wives when she was with him on his bed and she drew back:

> مَا لَكَ أَنْفَسْتَ ؟ قالت نعم

What is the matter with you? Have you begun to bleed? She said: Yes. He meant that she had menstruated.

Likewise the mustahadah — she is the woman whose blood does not cease, though it is distinguishable from menstrual blood. When her menstruation is upon her, the blood comes thick and turbid; when it departs, the blood becomes thin. What is binding upon her is this: as long as the menstrual blood is with her, she is in a state of menstruation — she does not pray, does not enter the mosque, and her husband may not approach her. When the menstrual blood departs and the remaining flow thins, she purifies herself as she purifies herself from menstruation; she is then in a state of purity, praying, fasting, entering the mosque, and her husband may come to her. Whenever any of that blood appears, she performs ablution, for it is an ailment affecting her.

It is reported from تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ — regarding the teaching that whoever approaches a menstruating woman has approached what is not lawful to him and has done what he ought not to do — that he must seek God's forgiveness and repent to Him for his offense, and if he gives charity alongside that, it is good. The blood of nifas is distinguishable from the blood of istihadah in the same way that menstrual blood is distinguishable from the blood of istihadah, as we mentioned. It is also reported from تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ: the same obligation applies to the woman if she consented; but if he compelled her, there is nothing upon her. If the man did not know of her menstruation and she concealed it from him until he had intercourse with her, the sin falls upon her and nothing upon him, since he did not know of her menstruation. The menstruating woman does not touch the mushaf.

It is said in the questions that came from the most venerable Shaykh Shimon ibn Muhammad Ghuri al-Hindi to our master Hasan ibn Idris, may God exalt his sanctity.

Question: What do you say, O support of the Dawa, concerning the term of nifas? The common people claim that the limit — both its minimum and its maximum — is forty days.

Answer: It may be less than forty days, except that forty days must be reckoned. And you asked, O magnificent master and forbearing scholar, about menstruation that exceeds ten days: if it exceeds ten days, she is a mustahadah. Our master and mawla, the dear father Muhammad ibn al-Fahd, may God exalt his sanctity, used to say that if a woman sees blood after ten days of her menstruation she is a mustahadah. She washes for each prayer time if she is able, and prays. If she cannot wash, she performs tayammum and prays. If she can wash at one time but not at another, she does so when she is able; and when she is unable, she performs tayammum for that time and prays and fasts.

It is said in the book of the question that came from the most venerable Shaykh Shimon ibn Muhammad Ghuri al-Hindi (رض), together with the answer of our master, the moon of the world and of religion, Hasan ibn Idris, may God exalt his sanctity and grant us his intercession and his company.

Question: What do you say concerning the one in a state of janaba, and the menstruating woman, who recites supplications or other texts containing something of the Quran — whether the reciter knows this or does not? How is such a person to act: does he recite it or leave it? For it is established in the radiant Sharia that neither of these two recites the Quran nor touches it. And may the one in a state of janaba, or the menstruating woman, recite the tahlil, the takbir, the tahmid, and the tasbih, given that all of these appear in the Quran? And may such a person recite the basmala, given that it has been said to be a verse of the Quran?

Answer: The menstruating woman does not recite the Quran, nor does the one in a state of janaba, nor any portion of it — whether in supplication or in books. Nor does such a person recite the basmala with the intention of reciting the Quran.

> فَتَحَقَّقْ مَا ذَكَرْتُهُ لَكَ أَيُّهَا الْأَخُ وَكُنْ مِنَ الْمُوقِنِينَ وَأعْبُدْ رَبَّكَ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَكَ الْيَقِينُ

Hold fast to everything I have set before you, brother — be among those who know with certainty, and worship your Lord until that certainty comes to you.

I turn now to istibra, the clearing of the womb, and I will say what appears in the book of questions and answers I have already cited:

> مَنْ زَنَى بِامْرَأَةٍ بِكْرًا أَوْ ثَيِّبًا فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَهَا فَلَا يَجُوزُ الْعَقْدُ اِلَّا بَعْدَ الِاسْتِبْرَاءِ

Whoever commits fornication with a woman — virgin or previously married — and then wishes to marry her: the marriage contract is not permitted until her womb has been cleared.

The book الْاِقْتِصَارُ records the following: if a man has a wife who has a child by another man, and that child dies leaving property, her husband withdraws from her until her womb is cleared. If she is pregnant, the child in the womb inherits from the deceased, provided his mother does not inherit from him; otherwise, nothing is cast into the womb that has no right in the inheritance. This applies when the mother is a slave or a polytheist. If she is a free Muslim woman, his inheritance belongs to her rather than to the brothers, and she does not withdraw.

The book مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ states that the woman undergoing the clearing of the womb withdraws for two months. The book كِتَابُ الْأَخْبَارِ records two transmitted positions: that a woman who has reached maturity but has not menstruated is cleared by forty-five nights; and that a virgin who reaches maturity, has not menstruated, and is then deflowered by the seller is cleared by nine months.

The book كِتَابُ الزِّينَةِ, concerning the saying:

> اَلْوَلَدُ لِلْفِرَاشِ وَلِلْعَاهِرِ الْحَجَرُ

He said: what is meant is only that the fornicator has no right in the lineage of the child.

The book of questions and answers already mentioned states: whoever commits fornication with a man's slave girl and then buys her from him while she is pregnant may not approach her until she gives birth. If she bears a child, its sale is permitted — even though the child came from him — because الْوَلَدُ لِلْفِرَاشِ، وَلِلزَّانِي الْحَجَرُ.

edits.chapter_key: gold, herds, and harvest
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the zakat of gold, silver, and jewels.

### Mentioning Zakat on Gold, Silver, and Jewels

He said in the book of questions and answers, arranged according to the order of the chapters of the Pillars of Islam:

Question: What do you say about a man who died having appointed two guardians, and one of them — or another of those close to the deceased — feared that the second guardian would block payment of what was owed from the estate: the khums, zakat, Hajj, and the rest? He paid these obligations in secret, without informing the second guardian, out of fear of him. Is anything held against him for that? And what must be paid, given that the deceased fixed nothing and left the matter unspecified, while the state of the kinsfolk is as it is, and it was known of him that he had withheld zakat, had not paid the khums on all his wealth, and had not performed the Hajj?

Answer: If the guardian discharges what lies upon the deceased, there is nothing wrong with it. Zakat is a debt from which release must first be obtained, then the Hajj, then the khums. If the next of kin do not obtain that release, nothing falls upon anyone else, as long as they clear his neck — whether in secret or openly.

Question: What do you say about a man who does not bring out the zakat of his wealth and does not deliver it to the one appointed to receive it? Is it permissible to eat food in his house?

Answer: There is nothing wrong with that.

Question: What do you say about a man who possessed wealth, did not pay its khums, and then died? Must the khums be taken from his entire estate — including the houses, the servants, and the undivided holdings — or not?

Answer: Yes, the khums is taken from his entire estate.

Question: What do you say about a man who owned the nisab and did not pay its zakat, or who did not own the nisab until he died, and then when his estate was assessed — goods and houses together — it was found to have reached the nisab? Must zakat be taken from it? And likewise, what of the Hajj and the other obligations that rested upon his wealth?

Answer: If what he left behind includes trade goods held for selling, buying, and commerce, and those goods reach the nisab, then paying their zakat is obligatory, and the Hajj is discharged after the zakat.

Question: What do you say about a man who died, and when his entire estate was examined it proved sufficient to cover the Hajj and the other obligations — expiation, al-Shurwa, and khums — even though during his lifetime the deceased had owned little beyond his house and its furnishings? Are the Hajj and the other obligations to be discharged while the heirs take what remains?

Answer: If he leaves wealth, the Hajj takes precedence over the inheritance, because it is a debt, and debt comes before inheritance. The remaining obligatory duties are likewise binding if the wealth is sufficient for them and something is still left for the heir.

Question: The collector of the customs levy takes ten dirhams from every two hundred dirhams paid by polytheists, and five dirhams from every two hundred dirhams paid by Muslims. The collector remitted one or two dirhams for certain Muslims. Now the owner of cloth for whom the collector remitted nothing comes to the man for whom he did remit, so that the goods may be registered in that man's name, on the condition that whatever remains is divided equally between the two of them. Is it permissible to take that arrangement or not?

Answer: Whatever the partners have agreed upon and both know of is permissible.

Question: A man died and left two hundred dinars — or less, or more — and zakat, Hajj, khums, al-Shurwa, and expiation were all owed from his estate. Which of these claims is settled first from the capital?

Answer: He begins with the zakat, for it is a debt upon him and is not part of his wealth; then the Hajj, then the khums, then the expiation, then al-Shurwa.

Question: A man died leaving wealth and an heir, and made no bequest at all. Are the khums, al-Shurwa, and the expiation taken from the capital or not?

Answer: The khums must be brought out of the capital. If the heirs are God-fearing, it is their duty to discharge it on behalf of the one who has passed, and so to purify the wealth. If they refuse, then:

> لَآ إِكْرَاهَ فِى ٱلدِّينِ

There is no compulsion in religion.

From another source: whoever pays the zakat of two years to the one authorized to receive it before the second year falls due, it is discharged from him.

Question: A man has two hundred mithqals and brings out the zakat at the head of the hawl. He then leaves one hundred in his house — neither selling nor buying with it — while he trades with the remaining hundred. When the second hawl comes round, does he pay zakat on the two hundred or on the one hundred? And likewise, if he buys a commodity and the hawl passes over it while he has not sold it, and the price has fallen: is zakat due on it or not?

Answer: Zakat remains obligatory on whatever it fell due on for as long as it stays with its owner — whether he trades with it or hoards it — until what he owns falls below the nisab.

Question: It appears in al-Masail that al-Shurwa is one hundred and nineteen dirhams, and that those of means owe a dinar. O our master, what is the limit of means, and what is the weight of a dinar, and what is the weight of a dirham?

Answer: Our master said: the limit of means, for all, is ownership of wealth on which zakat falls due after the hawl — that is, either two hundred dirhams or twenty gold dinars. Each dirham is fourteen carats of silver and two fifths of a carat; by this reckoning, the weight of two hundred dirhams is eighteen ounces by the weights of the Arabs, which is ninety-five kadiyana and a quarter kadiyana, and a wal and a quarter wal of silver by the weights of Gujarat. One then looks at what this silver is worth in the coinage current at the time. Whoever owns this amount, or more, is counted among those of means.

As for gold: each dinar is twenty-four carats, and by this reckoning the weight of twenty dinars is three ounces of gold by the weights of the Arabs, which is sixteen kadiyana less a wal and half a wal of gold. Yet here there is a matter to consider, because the price of gold and silver differs in every age according to people's desire for the one and their lack of desire for the other, and the reverse — so that at times the price of twenty dinars is more than two hundred dirhams, and at other times the opposite. It is therefore fitting for the believer who holds to his religion to reckon by whichever of the two named coinages — gold and silver — is the lesser in price.

Question: A man has five hundred tankas and brings out the fifth — one hundred tankas — in the first year, leaving him four hundred tankas. He traded with them and gained three hundred tankas in profit, of which household expenses took two hundred tankas, leaving him one hundred of the profit. Does he bring the khums out of three hundred tankas or out of one hundred?

Answer: If he has already brought out the khums from the capital, then there is no khums on the profit except on what remains in his hand. Paying khums on the whole is a merit, not a binding obligation.

This is the answer of our master Idris.

He said in Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: zakat is obligatory when what is liable to it reaches its nisab unencumbered and the hawl has passed over it. He said in it: as for a deposit, if the one holding it alters it and introduces into it what takes it out of the ruling of a deposit, or consumes it and puts wealth of his own in its place, then zakat on all of that is obligatory upon him. And if the hawl passes over the estate of a dead man after he has died and his heirs have not divided it, zakat is not obligatory on the estate as a whole, but is obligatory upon each of the shares: whoever's share reaches a nisab must pay zakat on it, and whoever's share does not reach a nisab — and who has no other wealth besides — owes no zakat on it. If a man has wealth and also owes a debt, and the hawl passes over it, one looks at what he owes and what he has; if his wealth exceeds his debt by a nisab or more, the zakat on the excess over his debt is binding upon him. If a man sells trade goods for the trade goods of another — which he also buys for trade — the second goods are valued at the head of the hawl reckoned from the time he first owned the original goods; and whether he suffered a loss in that or not, he pays what is due from him in zakat.

He said in it: likewise, if he buys trade goods with coin on which zakat is due, the reckoning follows how long the money and the goods stood in his hands; and when the hawl passes over it, he pays the zakat on his wealth.

He said in al-Akhbar: they narrated that whoever sets aside wealth that is surplus to him and then finds it again pays zakat on it. And from it: the apostate begins his zakat anew and does not pay zakat for what was his during his apostasy. He said: there is no zakat in the wealth of an orphan, nor in the wealth of one who lacks his reason.

Tawil al-Daaim said: this means that there is no zakat on that wealth due from the owner who holds it for himself; but whatever of it is held for trade is valued at a price, and zakat is due on it.

He said in Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: in what comes out of a mine there is the khums, and the remainder is for the one who found it; in buried treasure there is the khums; and dinars found bearing the coinage of Islam fall under the ruling of found property.

Some of the friends of God (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said: al-Shurwa due from the rich man of means is one hundred and nineteen mithqals of gold, and from the one without means, one hundred and nineteen pieces of silver.

He said in the questions put by our master Sulayman ibn Hasan in his early days, with the answers of our master Daud ibn 'Ajab: I also asked about one who has paid the khums of the lands of his estate — is the khums then due upon their seed or not?

Answer: Yes, may God prolong you; the khums is obligatory upon him in the seed of those lands, as God Almighty said:

> وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّمَا غَنِمْتُم مِّن شَيْءٍ فَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ

Know that whatever you take as spoil, a fifth of it belongs to God.

These seeds fall under the word "thing," as our master the Qadi al-Numan ibn Muhammad mentioned and made clear and plain in Kitab al-Himma.

He said in Tawil al-Sharia: Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah (ع) was asked about zakat, and he said that it is five dirhams, and that the poor are of five classes, with a dirham for each class. Zakat, he said, is mutual consolation: all people and the whole of creation are as a single soul, and when one limb of the body suffers pain, all the limbs turn to that limb to treat it until its pain is gone. When God tests one of the children of the human kind, it is the duty of the kind to occupy itself with his healing. And a man was mentioned in his presence, and it was said, "There is no defect in him." He (ع) said:

> لَوْ كَانَ أَحَدٌ لَمْ يَمْسَسْهُ عَيْبٌ لَمَا أَدْرَكَهُ الْمَوْتُ

If there were anyone whom no defect had touched, death would never have reached him.

Our master, the most exalted summoner, Jafar son of our master Mansur al-Yaman, said at the beginning of the Book of the Inner Nursing: the five prayers are known at five times, and the zakat likewise is five:

1. The khums of every wealth a man earns through trade, sales, and gain.
2. The zakat of wealth whose khums has already been brought out, which is one dinar from every forty dinars; it is an obligation due to the Hujja, and the khums is for the Imam.
3. The zakat of crops, which is likewise its tenth.
4. The zakat of livestock, which is one head from every forty head.
5. The zakat of the soul, which is what the believer pays for himself: the shurwa for the redemption of his neck, and the fitra of his fast — after these four obligatory zakats.

Our master Zayd ibn Muhammad said in al-Risala al-Maknuna: whoever owns twenty mithqals of gold owes half a mithqal. Then he said: and upon whoever owns two hundred dirhams there are five dirhams, and the two hundred are two covenants. He said in it: there is no zakat upon one who does not own twenty mithqals, nor upon one who does not own two hundred dirhams. He said in it: whoever owns two hundred dirhams is forbidden to take zakat and charity. He said in it: the owner of gold and silver owes no zakat on his wealth so long as the hawl has not passed over it.

### Mentioning Zakat on Livestock

He said in Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: there is no zakat on livestock until they are free-grazing and the hawl has passed over them. If they graze during part of the hawl and are fed with fodder during another part, the ruling follows whichever is the greater part.

He said in it: if someone owns five camels and fails to pay their zakat for two consecutive hawls, he owes a sheep for the first hawl but nothing for the second, since that second sheep already stands against him as a debt. The same principle applies to all livestock other than camels. If a man's camels have reached the threshold where camels are themselves the due, and he also owns sheep, then the zakat is taken from his sheep — from animals fit to serve as sacrificial animals — and the same applies to the zakat on sheep. Buffaloes and cows are alike in their zakat, as are sheep and goats.

He said in Tawil al-Daaim: this applies specifically when zakat has actually fallen due; if nothing has yet become due on them, then no obligation rests on him.

Our master Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman stated at the opening of the Book of the Inner Nursing: the zakat on livestock is one head from every forty.

Our master Zayd ibn Muhammad said in al-Risala al-Maknuna: camels are slaughtered by the thrust to the throat and then by the cut. He said in it: no zakat is due on fewer than five camels. He said in it: until the five are complete; and once he owns them, a sheep of the flock is obligatory — one sheep for every five — until they reach twenty, when he pays four sheep. When they reach twenty-five, a bint makhad is due. He said in it: the bint makhad is one whose mother has carried a young one in her belly. He said in it: then with an increase of ten; when they reach thirty-five, a bint labun is due. He said in it: when they reach forty-five, he pays a hiqqa fit to be covered by the stallion. He said in it: then with an increase of fifteen; and when one is added above sixty, a jadha is due. He said in it: above the jadha, nothing further is taken in charity. He said in it: a hiqqa was set at sixty camels because she resembles the stallion and is able to bear what he bears. He said in it: when the camels reach one hundred and twenty, two hiqqas are due, because one hundred and twenty is twice sixty.

He said in it: when cattle reach thirty, a tabi is due. He said in it: when they reach forty, a musinna is due. He said in it: in sixty, two tabis are due. He said in it: in ninety, three yearlings are due. He said in it: when they reach one hundred and twenty, in every forty a musinna is due and in every thirty a tabi.

He said in it, concerning sheep: when they reach forty, one sheep is due as charity. He said in it: up to one hundred and twenty, one sheep remains due. He said in it: when they reach two hundred, two sheep are due. He said in it: then after that, one sheep for every hundred. He said in it: nothing defective is taken in charity. He said in it: the ram of the flock is not taken in charity unless the collector wishes it.

### Mentioning Zakat on Grains, Fruits, and Plants

He said in the book of questions and answers mentioned above:

Question: The nisab of gold is twenty dinars and of silver two hundred dirhams. How then is the nisab of grains reckoned?

Answer: It has come in the Pillars that zakat is due from everything the earth brings forth, and upon this rests the practice of our masters, so it is a duty to follow them. They brought out the tenth from little and from much, and in that is merit. And it has come in the Sharia that the nisab in grains is five awsaq, and the wasq is sixty sa.

He said in al-Akhbar: whatever is sold as a standing crop — that is, grain — has zakat due on it; but whatever is sold before it forms its kernel and is then harvested carries no zakat. The same holds for fruits. They also narrated that the owner of the land does not set off against it what he spent upon it.

He said in Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: this is obligatory upon the young and the old, the rich and the poor, and upon one who is in debt.

From al-Akhbar: they narrated that the land of the tenth is every tract of Arab land against which the Muslims did not advance with horse or riding beast, and every mountain land that its own people brought into cultivation and which no water from the great rivers overflowed. That is the land of the tenth. They narrated that the land of kharaj is the land of the Sudan and those mountain lands against which the Muslims advanced with horse and riding beast and which they brought under cultivation by force. When the people of war submit while still upon their own territory, that land becomes land of the tenth. They further narrated that if a Muslim buys land of kharaj from a protected non-Muslim and takes possession of it, its ruling is not changed by passing to the Muslim, and it remains land of kharaj as it was; and if a protected non-Muslim buys land of the tenth from a Muslim and takes possession of it, the tenth is still due on what it brings forth, because that obligation attaches to the land's produce and no account is taken of the owner.

He said in Maalim al-Din: zakat is obligatory in all grains that run in the course of wheat and dates, and nothing of that reaches the measure unless it reaches five awsaq.

He said in al-Muntakhaba: the nisab of the grains we have mentioned is five awsaq, and the wasq is sixty sa.

He said in al-Akhbar: if part of a crop is watered by one means and part of it by another, the ruling follows whichever portion is the greater; and if the two are equal, three quarters of the tenth are taken from him. He said in it: one half is not joined to another half among grains and fruits, and there is no zakat in any of them until the half reaches the measure at which zakat becomes obligatory.

He said in Mukhtasar al-Athar: the tenth becomes obligatory in grains only when they form their kernels, and at that point an estimate is made — which is when their soundness becomes apparent — and a just estimate is made upon their owners.

He said in the Book of the Inner Nursing: as for the tenth, it is an outward ruling by which the Messenger of God judged, taken from the believers and from the people of the outward. He said in it: likewise, in the outward, whoever pays the tenth of his earnings in truth has rightly discharged his outward obligation, so long as he has kept back only nine tenths; he has done what he was told to do, even if the ruler over his outward affairs had made no demand of him. And whoever withholds some of his earnings and keeps with himself more than nine tenths has not rightly fulfilled what he intended by paying the tenth that was commanded of him, and has not in truth rendered obedience to the ruler over his outward affairs.

Our master Zayd ibn Muhammad said in al-Risala al-Maknuna: these five — meaning dates, raisins, wheat, barley, and grain — when they reach five awsaq, half a wasq of charity is due on them. He said in it: the tenth is obligatory on what the sky waters and what the rivers water; and on what is watered by wheels and by water-carrying beasts, half the tenth is due. He said in it: God imposed the khums on spoils. God Almighty said:

> وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّمَا غَنِمْتُم مِّن شَيْءٍ فَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ وَلِلرَّسُولِ وَلِذِي الْقُرْبَىٰ وَالْيَتَامَىٰ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ

Know that whatever you take as spoil, a fifth of it belongs to God, and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer.

These are five stations to which the khums is directed. He said in it: the khums is taken from mines, from treasures, and from spoils.

And from Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq (ع) it is transmitted that he said:

> كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَآلِهِ إِذَا أَتَاهُ الْمَغْنَمُ أَخَذَ نَصِيبَهُ ثُمَّ يَقْسِمُ مَا بَقِيَ بَيْنَ الْقُرْبَى وَالْيَتَامَى وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ

When spoils came to the Messenger of God, he would take his share and then distribute what remained among the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.

edits.chapter_key: a shield against the fire
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the Book of Fasting, and to the obligation of fasting the month of Ramadan.

He stated in the book Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: fasting is a shield from the Fire — a shield upon the tongues, the hearing, the eyes, and all the other limbs. It is not a matter of food and drink alone; every limb has its own portion in the fast, and whoever fulfills that portion is truly fasting. Whoever abandons any part of it diminishes the merit of his fast in proportion to what he has left. Fasting the month of Ramadan is an obligation upon every Muslim who is of age, sound of mind, healthy, and resident — and upon every woman likewise. He also stated therein: there is no fasting for one who is a hypocrite, disobedient to God.

He stated in the book al-Idah: what has come concerning fasting upon the sighting of the crescent, and what is mentioned in this chapter and in the two chapters before it, applies only to one who is absent from the presence of the Imam and does not know the measures of the crescents.

Our master and Mawlana Jafar ibn Sayyidina Sulayman, may God exalt his sanctity, stated in his noble epistle entitled The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations, in which he counseled his people and roused those among them who had grown heedless and whose sleep had lengthened — from the people of the island of Yemen, while he dwelt there and settled among them:

"Chapter: Among these matters also is what has been heard and known from most of you: that the honored month of Ramadan is not honored with the honor that God, glorified be He, and His Messenger (ع) have prescribed for it. It is the month of God, the Great, the Generous. That honor lies in placing the word 'month' before it, as God, glorified be He, said concerning it:

> شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ

The month of Ramadan.

Yet you, when you name it, call it 'Ramadan' alone, and that is never seemly in the judgment of the intellect, nor does it guide in this matter toward right guidance — for a person does not address one who is dear to him among people except with a word he places before his name, according to what is known among you and whose glory and form are recognized, together with what is established by the aforementioned word of God, glorified be He:

> وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ ٱلْأُمُورُ

And to God all matters return.

Beyond this, it has come concerning it from our master al-Qadi al-Numan ibn Muhammad, may God exalt his sanctity, in the book Mukhtasar al-Athar al-Sharif, that your Mawla the Imam al-Baqir Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) said:

> لَا تَقُولُونَ رَمَضَانَ وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا كَمَا قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى شَهْرَ رَمَضَانَ

Do not say Ramadan, but say as God Almighty said: the month of Ramadan.

So whoever has had God, glorified be He, cause his ear to hear this saying — how can it be permissible for him to oppose it and turn away from it, being of the people of piety and faith? The heedless one who turns away from it after having come to stand upon it makes light of God, glorified be He, and of His noble month mentioned above, and of the weighty saying of the Imam al-Baqir (ع) mentioned above. And the one who speaks by this noble book while turning away from acting upon what is in it enters under the censure contained in the words of God, glorified be He, in the verses of His noble and guarded Book, where He, glorified be He, says:

> يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لِمَ تَقُولُونَ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ
>
> كَبُرَ مَقْتًا عِندَ اللَّهِ أَن تَقُولُوا مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ

O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? It is greatly hateful in the sight of God that you say what you do not do."

He stated in the book Tawil al-Shariah: fasting becomes obligatory upon a boy once he can tell his right hand from his left.

He stated in the fourteenth majlis of the Mustansiriyya councils, God's peace be upon its author: what follows is what we recite to you concerning the meaning of fasting, and that it is divided into categories, of which seven are obligatory and twelve are of the practice and commended. The obligatory ones are:

1. Fasting the month of Ramadan every year.
2. Fasting two consecutive months for one who deliberately breaks his fast on a day of it and cannot find a slave to free.
3. Fasting two consecutive months for one who kills a believer by mistake, if he likewise cannot find a slave to free, together with paying the blood money to the family.
4. In the expiation of zihar, fasting two consecutive months for one who cannot find a slave to free.
5. In the expiation for breaking an oath, fasting three days for one who can find neither the feeding nor the clothing nor the freeing of a slave.
6. The fast of one who performs tamattu with the lesser pilgrimage up to the pilgrimage, when he cannot find an offering, and it is ten days.
7. The fast of a vow.

As for the fasts of the practice and the commended:

1. The fast of itikaf.
2. The fast of Shaban.
3. The fast of the first Thursday of every month.
4. The fast of the middle Wednesday of that month.
5. The fast of the last Thursday of that month.
6. The fast of the three white days.
7. The fast of Dawud (ع), which is fasting one day and breaking the fast the next, and it is the most rigorous of fasts.
8. The fast of Friday joined to Thursday or to Saturday, without singling out Friday alone for fasting.
9. The fast of the day of Arafah for one who is not on pilgrimage.
10. The fast of the boy when he reaches seven years.
11. The fast of recompense for game taken in the sacred state, which varies according to what is ruled by the one to whom God has entrusted the ruling in it.
12. The fast for shaving the head on account of harm.

Our master Zaid ibn Muhammad, may God sanctify his soul, stated in the Concealed Epistle: God Almighty imposed upon His servants, after the performance of prayer and the giving of zakat, the fasting of the month of Ramadan, and He commanded that one month out of twelve be fasted. He stated therein: just as the fasting of the month of Ramadan is obligatory, it is thirty days.

Mawlana Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع) stated in his Four Hundred Manners:

> صَوْمُ ثَلَاثَةِ أَيَّامٍ مِنْ كُلِّ شَهْرٍ وَصَوْمُ شَعْبَانَ يُذْهِبُ بِوَسْوَاسِ الصَّدْرِ وَبَلَابِلِ الْقَلْبِ

Fasting three days of every month, and fasting Shaban, drive away the whisperings of the breast and the disquiet of the heart.

edits.chapter_key: three questions from the king of rum
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the guardianship of the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), and to his love and his station.

Our master and Mawlana, the long-serving preacher Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman — may God exalt him, sanctify him, and grant us his intercession and his blessing — said in the Book of the Foster-Suckling that Muhammad is His prophet, and that God says of him:

> فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ مَوْلَىٰهُ وَجِبْرِيلُ وَصَلِحُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
>
> "Indeed God is his master, and Gabriel, and the righteous of the believers."

By this is meant the Imam of the believers, who is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Imam of every believing man and every believing woman. And His words:

> وَكَانَ أَبُوهُمَا صَلِحًۭا
>
> "And their father was righteous."

By this is meant an Imam. And His words:

> أَنَّ ٱلْأَرْضَ يَرِثُهَا عِبَادِىَ ٱلصَّلِحُونَ
>
> "The earth is inherited by My righteous servants."

By this are meant the Imams from among His servants.

Mawlana the Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah (ع) said in his supplication for Sunday, likening himself in the physical world to a pen in the spiritual world. He set four ranks beneath it, each one preceded by a spiritual rank that guides it toward the rank beyond. In this way he established the foundation facing the tablet, engraving into it what he derived from the spiritual world, just as a pen engraves upon a tablet.

I now record the answers given by the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), to questions he was asked, and what followed from them.

It is stated in the book Uns al-Afidah al-Muniba, in the account of some of the cases of the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع) and his remarkable rulings:

The king of Rum sent a messenger to Medina with a sum of money and instructed him: "Go to Muhammad. If you do not reach him, then ask about his successor, and put to him proof." The messenger was to ask three questions, and if he received answers, he was to hand over the money.

The man arrived in Medina, but the Messenger of God (ع) had already passed away. He asked about his successor and was directed to Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr was brought forward, and the man asked him: "Tell me what is not God, what is not with God, and what God does not know." Abu Bakr grew angry and said to him: "Woe to you. By saying this you have added to your disbelief." The man left his presence. He was then directed to 'Umar, who responded in much the same way.

Then 'Abdullah ibn Abbas said: "What kind of men are these? They could not answer his questions, and yet they did not simply say, We do not know.' Instead they accused him of knowing falsehood. I know who knows the answer." He was asked, "Who is he?" He said, "'Ali ibn Abi Talib." They said, "Take us to him," and they all set out together with the man and knocked on his door.

The Commander of the Faithful (ع) came out to them with a pen behind his ear and his finger stained with ink. 'Abdullah ibn Abbas told him the story, and he (ع) said to the man: "Ask what you wish." The man said: "Tell me what is not God's." He said: "God has no partner." He said: "Tell me what is not with God." He said: "Injustice." He said: "Tell me what God does not know." He said: "That the Messiah is the son of God. For God Almighty, glorified and exalted be His name, has said:

> أَتُنَبِّـُٔونَ ٱللَّهَ بِمَا لَا يَعْلَمُ

'Do you inform God of what He does not know?'"

The meaning is that it does not exist, and God has no knowledge of what does not exist.

The man said: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and that you are his guardian." He then handed over the money, and 'Ali (ع) gave it to al-Hasan and al-Husayn (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) and told them: "Go and distribute it among the Muslims," and they did as he commanded.

It is also narrated from Abu al-Jarud, from al-Harith al-Awar, that while the Commander of the Faithful (ع) was in al-Rahba with the people pressing around him — some seeking a ruling, others seeking help — a man stood and addressed him: "Peace be upon you, O Commander of the Faithful, and the mercy and blessings of God." The Commander of the Faithful (ع) looked at him and said: "And upon you peace, and the mercy and blessings of God. Who are you?" He said: "A man from your flock and from the people of your country."

He said to him, "You are neither of my flock nor of the people of my country. If you had greeted me for a single day, you would not be hidden from me." Then he said to those around him: "Do you know this man?" No one knew him. So he said to the man, "These are the people of your country, and they do not know you. Had I seen you for a single day, you would not be hidden from me." The man said, "Safety, O Commander of the Faithful." He said, "Have you committed any transgression in this land of mine since you entered it?" He said, "No." He said, "Perhaps during the days of war?" He said, "Yes." He said, "When war lays down its burdens, there is no harm in it."

The man said: "Muawiya sent me to you and commanded me to come to you unannounced, to ask you about things that Ibn al-Asfar sent to him to inquire about. He says to him: if you are the rightful guardian of this matter and the claimant of the caliphate after Muhammad, then answer me these things, for if you answer me I will follow you and send you the tribute. And when the messenger saw that he had no answer to them, he sent me to you to ask you about them."

He said, "And what are they?" The man said:

- How great is the distance between truth and falsehood?
- How great is the distance between heaven and earth?
- How great is the distance between east and west?
- What is this galaxy?
- What is the rainbow?
- What is the darkening in the moon?
- What is the first thing that appeared on the face of the earth?
- What is the first thing that stirred upon it?
- What is the spring to which the souls of the polytheists flee?
- What is the hermaphrodite?
- What are the ten things, each harder than the last?

The Commander of the Faithful (ع) said to him: "God has destroyed the son of the liver-eater. How astray he is, and how astray are those with him. By God, he freed his slave girl and did not do well to marry her. God judge between me and this nation, who severed my ties of kinship, wasted my days, denied me my right, diminished the greatness of my station, and joined together in contending against me."

Then he said, "Bring me al-Hasan, al-Husayn, and Muhammad." They came to him. He said to the man, "O brother of the people of Syria, these are the sons of the Messenger of God (ع)," and he gestured toward al-Hasan and al-Husayn (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), "and this is my son," and he gestured toward Muhammad (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْه), "so ask whichever of them you wish." The Syrian said he wished to ask al-Hasan (ع). The Commander of the Faithful (ع) said to him, "Ask him," and he asked him all of those questions.

Al-Hasan (ع) said: "O brother of the people of Syria, the distance between truth and falsehood is four fingers. What your eyes see is truth, and with your ears you may hear a great deal of falsehood." The Syrian said, "You have spoken truly, may God set you aright."

He said: "Between heaven and earth lies the prayer of the oppressed and the reach of sight. Whoever says otherwise has lied." He said, "You have spoken truly."

He said: "Between east and west lies the sun's course in a single day. You look at it as it rises and you look at it as it sets. Whoever says otherwise has lied." He said, "You have spoken truly."

He said: "As for this galaxy, it is the lamps of the sky, and from it the pouring water descends. As for the rainbow, it is the bow of God and a safeguard from drowning. As for the darkening in the moon: the moon's light was once like the light of the sun, but God blotted it out. God, mighty and majestic, said regarding that:

> وَجَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهَارَ آيَتَيْنِ فَمَحَوْنَا آيَةَ اللَّيْلِ وَجَعَلْنَا آيَةَ النَّهَارِ مُبْصِرَةً

'And We made the night and the day two signs, and We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible.'

As for the first thing that appeared on the face of the earth, it is the valley of Dab. As for the first thing that stirred upon the face of the earth, it is the palm tree. As for the spring to which the souls of the polytheists flee, it is a spring called Salma. As for the hermaphrodite, it is a human being of whom it is not known whether the person is a woman or a man; so the person is examined: if a man, he has the emission of a man; and if a woman, she menstruates or her breasts develop. Otherwise the person is told to urinate against a wall: if the urine strikes the wall, it is a man, and if it falls back as the urine of a camel falls back, it is a woman. As for the ten things, each harder than the last: the hardest thing God created is stone; harder than stone is iron, by which stone is cut; stronger than iron is fire; stronger than fire is water; stronger than water is cloud; stronger than cloud is wind; stronger than wind is the angel; stronger than the angel is the Angel of Death; more severe than the Angel of Death is death itself; and more severe than death is the command of God, Lord of all worlds."

Then the Syrian said, "I bear witness that you are the son of the Messenger of God (ع), and that 'Ali (ع) is the guardian of Muhammad (ع), and that he has more right to this affair than Muawiya." He wrote these things down and carried them to Muawiya, and Muawiya sent them to Ibn al-Asfar. Ibn al-Asfar said: "I bear witness that these are not from you, and that they come only from the mine of prophecy and the seat of the message. As for you, were you to ask me for a single dirham, I would not give it to you."

It is also narrated from him that he said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab came to the Commander of the Faithful (ع) and said to him, "O Abu al-Hasan, there are matters I neglected to ask the Messenger of God (ع) about. Do you have anything concerning them?"

He said, "And what are they?" He said: "A man lies down and sees something in his sleep, and when he awakens it is as though he had taken it in his hand; yet he may see something that turns out to be nothing at all. And a man meets another man and loves him without knowing him. And a man meets another man and hates him without knowing him. And a man sees a thing with his eye or hears it and remembers it for a long age, then forgets it at the moment he needs it, then recalls it when he has no need of it."

The Commander of the Faithful (ع) said to him concerning that: "As for what you say about the thing a man sees in his sleep, God, blessed and exalted, said in His noble Book:

> اللَّهُ يَتَوَفَّى الْأَنفُسَ حِينَ مَوْتِهَا وَالَّتِي لَمْ تَمُتْ فِي مَنَامِهَا فَيُمْسِكُ الَّتِي قَضَىٰ عَلَيْهَا الْمَوْتَ وَيُرْسِلُ الْأُخْرَىٰ إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى

'God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died, during their sleep. He keeps those for whom He has decreed death and releases the others until an appointed term.'

Every servant who lies down to sleep carries within him a likeness of death. Whatever he sees while resting, with his soul loosened from his body, is true — he is in the kingdom. Whatever he sees as his soul returns is false; that is the delusion of Shaytan. As for what you say about a man seeing another and loving him without knowing him, or hating him without knowing him — God, mighty and majestic, created the souls two thousand years before the bodies, settled them in the air, and they would meet and scent one another as horses scent one another. Whatever souls came to know one another on that day are joined together today and love; whatever souls rejected one another on that day are divided today and hate. As for what you say about a man seeing something with his eye or hearing it, then forgetting it, then recalling it, then forgetting it once more — there is no heart that does not have a film over it, like the film of the moon. When that film passes through the heart, the servant forgets what he has seen and heard."

At that, 'Umar said, "You have spoken truly, O Abu al-Hasan. May God not keep me alive after you, and may I never be in a land where you are not."

edits.chapter_key: forgetting, doubting, and beginning again
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the subject of omission in the prayer.

In the question-and-answer book I named at the outset — one of whose arrangers set out following the order of the chapters of the Book of the Pillars of Islam — the following is asked:

Question: What do you say if someone makes room for another to pray, standing in for a man who does not know all the positions in the prayer that require the prostration of omission? Must that man perform the two prostrations of omission after completing every obligatory act about which something appears uncertain to him, or not?

The answer is: if it is established that he has indeed committed an omission, he prostrates for it; otherwise he does not.

Question: What do you say regarding the statement in the Book of Purity that whoever errs by not pronouncing the opening takbir — or omits it deliberately or out of ignorance — must repeat the prayer? O our master, if a man forgets to open the prayer after every two rakahs in the four-rakah and six-rakah prayers, does that invalidate his prayer or not?

The answer is: if he did not sit after each pair of rakahs, his prayer is invalidated.

Question: What do you say regarding the statement in the Book of Purity that whoever inadvertently adds to his prayer, even without sitting for the tashahhud, must repeat the prayer; and that if he adds an extra bowing he repeats the prayer, but if he adds an extra prostration he completes the prayer and performs the two prostrations of omission? What does this mean?

The answer is: if he adds a bowing and has not sat for the tashahhud, he must repeat the prayer. But if he has sat for the tashahhud and completed two rakahs — whether with an additional bowing or an additional prostration — he has done so in order.

Question: What do you say about a man who is praying behind an Imam and neglects one of the pillars of the prayer while following the Imam? How is his prayer?

The answer is: the Imam bears the responsibility for the omission, except in the case of the bowing and the opening takbir — and the first thing is that he should not neglect those.

Question: What do you say regarding the statement in religious law that whoever forgets a prostration should prostrate after delivering the salaam, when he remembers? O our master, how does he prostrate after having left the prayer?

The answer is: he prostrates if he remembers before delivering the salaam. If he has already left the prayer, he has no recourse.

Question: What does our master say about a man who prayed the obligatory prayer and recited it in reverse order, from bottom to top? Must he perform the two prostrations of omission or not?

The answer is: there is nothing wrong with that, and it is not obligatory upon him to perform the two prostrations of omission.

Question: A man prayed some of the obligatory Zuhr prayer and sat down and recited the first tashahhud, then prayed two more rakahs and recited the tashahhud again, then recalled that he had prayed only three rakahs. What should he do?

The answer is: he prays the rakah he missed after the salaam, reciting in it the Opening and a surah, because it is one of the first two rakahs. He then recites the tashahhud, delivers the salaam, and performs the two prostrations of omission.

Question: Whoever neglects the first tashahhud in the obligatory prayer but recites the final tashahhud, then remembers before delivering the salaam — must he perform the prostration of omission or not?

The answer is: there is no explicit text on this, and where there is no text it has not been stipulated that the worshipper must prostrate.

Question: Regarding the man who repeats a single surah in the obligatory prayer after the Opening — must he perform the prostration of omission or not?

The answer is: this too has not been stipulated.

Question: Regarding a man who omits one obligation — should he prostrate the two prostrations of omission? And if he omits three obligations, does he prostrate separately for each omission with two prostrations, or do two prostrations suffice for all of them?

The answer is: the prostration of omission is not multiplied.

Question: Regarding a man who prays behind an Imam and forgets to intend in his prayer that he is a follower — if the Imam delivers the salaam of the dhikr and the man then remembers that he did not intend to follow him, is his prayer valid or not?

The answer is: if his intention was to follow the Imam, his prayer is complete, even though he did not utter it.

Question: What is transmitted from Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع), who said:

> مَنْ سَهَىٰ عَنِ الْقِرَاءَةِ فِي بَعْضِ الصَّلَاةِ فَقَرَأَ فِي مَا بَقِيَ مِنْهَا أَجْزَاَهُ ذَٰلِكَ فَإِنْ نَسِيَ الْقِرَاءَةَ كُلَّهَا وَأَتَمَّ الرُّكُوعَ وَالسُّجُودَ وَالتَّكْبِيرَ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلَيْهِ الْإِعَادَةُ

This statement presents no difficulty.

Question: If one forgets to recite some of the Quran, or all of it, must he perform the two prostrations of omission?

The answer is: the two prostrations of omission are required, and he performs them.

Question: What of a man whom the Imam has preceded in some part of the prayer? Must the latecomer perform the two prostrations of omission that the Imam himself owed before the latecomer arrived?

The answer is: whoever enters the prayer with the Imam prostrates those two prostrations for his Imam's omission — even if the only part he caught with him before the salaam was the opening takbir.

Question: In the case of one who was preceded and prays part of the prayer with the Imam, then makes an error in what remains upon him — must he prostrate for the omission?

The answer is: if he omits something while praying on his own, he prostrates.

Question: The text states that

> الْأَعْمَالُ لَا تُقْبَلُ اِلَّا بِالنِّيَّاتِ

deeds are accepted only with intentions. So if a person neglects — when purifying himself, or when beginning his prayer, or when fasting, or when performing any of the duties of God — to contract the intention with the tongue while he intends the act in his heart, is his action valid?

The answer is: the intention resides in the heart, and what is said with the tongue is merely a verbal expression, as mentioned in the Pillars. If he has contracted the intention in his heart, his act is complete.

He said in the councils of instruction that doubt in prayer has its root in omission, which is inattention. It is a word that troubles many of those who occupy themselves with jurisprudence, so that they suppose doubt to be like omission — but it is not so. The one who commits an omission is certain of what he has omitted, while the doubter is not certain of what he doubts.

Concerning the prostration of omission, it is said in the reports that it is performed after the salaam, and that after it one recites a brief testimony:

> بِسْمِ اللَّهِ وَبِاللَّهِ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا اِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَصَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ

In the name of God, and by God, and I bear witness that there is no god but God, and may God bless Muhammad and his family.

It is also said: whoever falls into doubt while praying and does not know whether he is in an obligatory prayer or a voluntary one — if he stood up for the prescribed prayer and then became inattentive afterward and supposed it to be voluntary, that prayer suffices him for the prescribed one and his inattention does no harm; but if he stood up for a voluntary prayer, then it is voluntary. It is said: whoever doubts and does not know whether he prayed Zuhr or Asr — if some of the time of Asr still remains, he prays it; but if the sun has set and he then doubts, no making up is due from him. It is said: if you doubt about the dawn prayer, pray it again; and if you doubt about the sunset prayer, pray it again. It is said: whoever commits omissions repeatedly in a single prayer owes nothing but the two prostrations of omission.

I find in the Mukhtasar al-Musannaf that if a man prays a four-rakah prayer and then, through inattention, rises for a fifth — if he had already recited the tashahhud in the fourth, he delivers the salaam while standing and departs; if he had not yet recited it, he sits, recites the tashahhud, and performs the two prostrations of omission. If he remembers that he rose to a fifth rakah only after he has bowed, and he had already recited the tashahhud in the fourth, his prayer is complete, and he joins to that rakah another as a voluntary prayer for himself; but if he had not recited the tashahhud in the fourth and did not sit for the length of the tashahhud, he repeats the prayer. Whoever forgets a prayer and does not know whether he prayed two, three, or four rakahs — and the Imam who prays aloud in what is prayed silently — has done ill, though his prayer is complete; and if he did that inattentively, the two prostrations of omission are upon him. If he is not an Imam but prays alone, and recites silently in what is recited aloud, or aloud in what is recited silently, nothing is due from him. Whatever holds concerning omission in the prayer of residence holds equally in the prayer of travel.

I find, in the questions put by certain of the ranks of the island of India — with their answers from certain of the summoners of the island of Yemen, may God sanctify all their souls — in the twenty-sixth issue: concerning the man who is inattentive in the recitation in the obligatory prayer and recites in the second rakah, after the first, a surah taken from above, which is not what is required in the obligatory prayer — are the two prostrations of omission upon him? The answer is: this has not been stipulated, and he should not do it deliberately. And in the first issue of that collection: the text states that deeds are accepted only with intentions — so if a person neglects, when purifying himself, or in his prayer, or in his fasting, or when performing any of the duties of God, to contract the intention with the tongue while he intends the act in his heart, is his action valid? And if he goes beyond that and abandons the intention of the tongue entirely, is his action valid? The answer is: the intention resides in the heart, and what is uttered on the tongue is merely a statement, as mentioned in the Pillars. If he has contracted the intention in his heart, his act is complete.

I find in the book on the interpretation of the Sharia that whoever misses a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it.

Our master, the owner of the Mustansiriyya councils, God's (ع), said in the ninth of them: Listen now to what we recite to you of the meaning of doubt and omission in the prayer. The places of omission in prayer are seven, in six of which the two prostrations of omission are proper. They are the two that rub down the nose (اَلْمُرْغِمَتَانِ), and they are so named because they rub down the nose of the devil when the corruption of forgetfulness is repaired by them. Of these:

1. Whoever is inattentive to a prostration prostrates when he remembers it, and the two prostrations of omission are upon him.
2. Whoever forgets to sit for the first tashahhud and stands for the third rakah, and remembers before he bows that he did not sit, sits and recites the tashahhud, and when he delivers the salaam he performs the two prostrations of omission.
3. If his inattention to the first tashahhud carries him on until he has bowed and prostrated, he completes his prayer, and the two prostrations of omission are upon him.
4. Whoever is inattentive to the second tashahhud and delivers the salaam owes the two prostrations of omission.
5. Whoever, through inattention, delivers the salaam after two rakahs when he is in a four-rakah prayer, prays two rakahs after them and performs the two prostrations of omission.
6. Whoever, through inattention, rises from the final tashahhud after completing it to a fifth rakah owes the two prostrations of omission.
7. Whoever is inattentive behind the Imam owes no prostration of omission, for the Imam bears that for him.

These are the seven places of omission in which the two prostrations are proper. As for doubt in prayer, it is a word that troubles many of those who occupy themselves with jurisprudence, so that they suppose it to be like omission — but it is not so. The one who commits an omission is certain of what he omitted, while the doubter is not certain of what he doubts. Doubt falls into twelve cases; in some of them there is a prostration of omission, and in others nothing at all. Those in which there is a prostration of omission are:

1. If the worshipper doubts about the bowing while he is still in the prayer, he bows, and the two prostrations of omission are upon him.
2. If he doubts and does not know whether he is in one rakah or two, he builds upon what is certain, and that is the lesser.
3. Likewise, if he doubts and does not know whether he has prayed two rakahs or three, he builds upon what is certain.
4. If he doubts and does not know whether he has prayed three or four, he delivers the salaam, prays two rakahs seated, and performs the two prostrations of omission.
5. If he does not know whether he has prayed two or four, he delivers the salaam, prays two rakahs standing, and performs the two prostrations of omission.

As for those in which nothing is due:

6. If the worshipper doubts about the opening takbir after he has bowed, he continues in his prayer and nothing is due from him.
7. Likewise if he doubts about the recitation after his bowing.
8. Likewise if he doubts about the bowing after his prostration.
9. Likewise if he doubts about the first prostration after his second prostration.
10. Likewise if he doubts about the prostration after the tashahhud.
11. Likewise if he doubts about anything of the prayer after the salaam.

In all of this nothing is due from him.

Our master, the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), said in his four hundred manners:

> مَنْ كَانَ عَلَى يَقِينِهِ فَأَصَابَهُ شَكٌّ فَلْيَمْضِ عَلَى يَقِينِهِ فَاِنَّ الشَّكَّ لَا يَدْفَعُ الْيَقِينَ وَلَا يَنْقُصُهُ

Whoever is certain of something and is then struck by doubt should act on his certainty, for doubt neither dispels certainty nor diminishes it.

Among the questions submitted by certain shaykhs of India — may God be pleased with them — along with answers from our masters the summoners of Yemen — may God exalt their sanctity and grant us their intercession and their nearness — is the following. Question: What do you say concerning a man who is inattentive in forming his intention and does not declare himself a follower? Is his prayer valid or not? Answer: If his intention was to follow the Imam, his prayer is complete, even though he did not utter it aloud.

In the book of questions, I was asked about one who doubts during his prayer and does not know how much of it he has performed. He builds on what he is certain of and then prostrates the two prostrations of omission after he delivers the salaam. If, however, he is certain of nothing — not knowing whether he added to or fell short of his prayer — he begins again from the beginning, and so likewise does the Imam.

I now turn to what interrupts the prayer.

In the question-and-answer book named at the outset, arranged according to the chapters of the book of the Pillars of Islam: whoever vomits during the prayer, and the vomit reaches his garment, should wash the garment if water is close at hand; otherwise his prayer is void, and he then washes his garment and prays again. Whoever breaks his purity before the tashahhud must repeat the prayer; and if he breaks it after he has said,

> اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ

"Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of God and His blessings; peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God" — his prayer is permitted, and he does not repeat it.

I mentioned in the Book of Purity that if a person suffers a nosebleed or vomits while in prayer, and can wash away the blood and stop the bleeding, and rinse away the vomit, all without turning his face from the qibla, he does so and builds upon his prayer. If he does turn his face from the qibla, however, he must repeat the prayer from its beginning. The reports add: unless he detects the breaking of purity — by finding its smell, hearing its sound, or having another person hear it from him.

I also mentioned in the book on the interpretation of prayer that the Prophet (ع) said:

> ثَلَاثٌ تَقْطَعُ الصَّلَاةَ الْمَرْأَةُ وَالْحِمَارُ وَالْكَلْبُ الْأَسْوَدُ

Three things interrupt the prayer: a woman, a donkey, and a black dog. There is also the report that the Messenger of God (ع) was standing in prayer when a dog passed before him, then a donkey passed, then a woman passed while he was praying; and when he had finished he said:

> رَأَيْتُ الَّذِي رَأَيْتُمْ وَلَيْسَ يَقْطَعُ صَلَاةَ الْمُؤْمِنِ شَيْءٌ وَلَكِنِ ادْرَءُوا مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ

I saw what you saw, and nothing interrupts the prayer of a believer; but ward off what you are able to ward off.

Our master, the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), said in his four hundred manners:

> لَا يَقْطَعُ الصَّلَاةَ التَّبَسُّمُ وَيَقْطَعُهَا الْقَهْقَهَةُ

Smiling does not interrupt the prayer, but loud laughter interrupts it.

It is mentioned in the book of questions — its question from the most honorable Shaykh Shimun ibn Muhammad Ghuri al-Hindi, and its answer from our master Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, may God exalt their sanctity and grant us their intercession and their nearness. Question: What do you say about a man who entered the obligatory prayer with the opening takbir and recited, and then the Imam arrived and came forward while the man was still standing; and when the Imam bowed, the man bowed with him without renewing the opening takbir? What is the state of his prayer? The answer: he must repeat it.

I come now to the prayer of one who has been preceded in part of the prayer.

It is mentioned in the question-and-answer book named at the outset, arranged according to the chapters of the book of the Pillars of Islam. Question: What do you say about a worshipper who reaches the Imam while the Imam is in the final tashahhud of any of the five prayers, the latecomer intending in his prayer to follow, sitting while the Imam sits, until when the Imam delivers the salaam of his prayer the latecomer rises and prays? Has the latecomer attained the congregation, and is his prayer valid? The answer: if he reached the Imam in the tashahhud — which is the last of the prayer's limits — he intends the prayer as a follower, sits, and makes the supplication of turning toward God; and when the Imam delivers the salaam, he rises and prays his prayer, and he has attained the prayer of the congregation.

It is mentioned in the book Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: if a latecomer reaches the Imam in the bowing, he says the takbir for the opening and then the takbir for the bowing, and that rakah is counted for him; and if he fears missing it, a single takbir suffices for both the opening and the bowing. Whoever reaches the Imam having been preceded enters into whatever the Imam is in — if it is something that is counted, he builds upon it; if not, he is one performing a voluntary act. He prays what he has caught and makes up what escaped him.

It is said in the reports concerning an Imam whose purity is broken, who then puts forward a man who has been preceded: if that man does not know what the Imam preceded him with, he proceeds on his certainty until those behind him say the glorification to him, and then he reverts accordingly.

Our master and lord Muhammad ibn Fahd, may God exalt his sanctity, said in his noble epistle, which he titled The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided, in the twentieth question: You asked also, may God grant you success in what pleases Him, about the latecomer who is unable to make the intention by uttering it with his tongue, and who enters with the Imam into whatever part of the prayer and its rakahs the Imam is in. The answer to you in this, by the granting of God — be He glorified — of what is correct in speech upon it, and its truth is thus: it has come in the books of the friends of God (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) that if the latecomer reaches the Imam in any rakah of his prayer and the Imam has not yet raised his head from the bowing in it, and the latecomer says a single takbir and enters with the Imam into his prayer by it, then he has attained that rakah with the Imam, and that is so together with the contracting of the intention in his heart upon it.

edits.chapter_key: the grammar of peace
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the guardianship of the Imams from the family of the Messenger of Allah (ع), and to the obligation of praying for Muhammad and the family of Muhammad (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) — together with what pertains to that prayer: the good proclaimers, the righteous borders, their stations, the command to return peace, and the reply to the greeting of the book.
