Question: What do you say concerning the teacher of boys, when he is teaching them the Quran and passes over the places of prostration while instructing them? Does he prostrate every time he passes over them, and do those who hear him prostrate as well, or not?

Answer: He has a choice in that: if he wishes, he prostrates, and if he wishes, he leaves it.

Another case: a man says in the prostration of the Quran what he says in the prostration of prayer.

It is said in مُخْتَصَرُ الْمُصَنَّفِ: when the reciter recites one of the binding prostrations, whoever is present prostrates. If that same prostration is recited again, none of them is required to prostrate a second time so long as he remains in that place. As for the remaining prostrations, whoever wishes to prostrate may prostrate, and whoever wishes may leave it; though prostrating is better.

Mawlana, the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), said in his four hundred points of conduct:

> أَطِيلُوا السُّجُودَ فَمَا مِنْ عَمَلٍ أَشَدُّ عَلَى إِبْلِيسَ مِنْ أَنْ يَرَى ابْنَ آدَمَ سَاجِدًا فَأَنَّهُ أُمِرَ بِالسُّجُودِ فَعَصَى وَأُمِرَ ابْنُ آدَمَ بِالسُّجُودِ فَأَطَاعَ وَنَجَا

Prolong the prostration, for nothing bears more heavily on Iblis than to see the son of Adam prostrating. He was himself commanded to prostrate and disobeyed, while the son of Adam was commanded to prostrate, obeyed, and was saved.

edits.chapter_key: washing, shrouding, carrying, burying
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the washing of the dead and to what belongs with it.

In the book of questions and answers arranged according to the order of the chapters of *The Pillars of Islam*, the following was asked. Question: what do you say concerning a man who washes the dead? Must he perform the ablution upon them three times together with three washings, or not? Answer: yes, he performs the ablution upon them three times together with three washings; and if he performs their ablution at the last of the washings, that suffices for them, as comes in the Book of Reports. From another place: if a man is wounded and is not moved from his place, and lives an hour, or two hours, or a day, and speaks, he is likewise not washed, because he was not lifted from his place.

Question: concerning one who dies while traveling and no water is to be found; or a man who dies among women with no woman of his own; or a woman who dies with no husband and no woman to be found who may wash her — must the dead in such cases be given tayammum with earth, or not? Answer: it is mentioned that if a man in a state of janabah and a dead person are together, and there is not enough water except for one of them, the man in janabah performs the washing and the dead is given tayammum; and these cases are like that. From another place: if a man dies, the washer washes the dead even while in janabah; and if washing would harm him, he performs tayammum and then washes the dead, and this is permitted when he finds no one else. And if the man in janabah is the more excellent of them, his washing of the dead is permitted.

It is said in the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif that the nearest of those present to the dead has the best right to wash him. From the same book: if the martyr was in janabah, he is washed on account of the janabah. And if a man is found dead with no mark upon him, he is washed, treated with hanut, and shrouded.

It is said in the Mukhtasar al-Athar that the drowned and the burned are washed, and so is a limb — when there is found of a man such a part that it is known he could not have lived once it was parted from him. Whatever falls from the dead is washed and placed with him. If his limbs, or any of them, have come apart, they are washed and each limb is set in its own place, and he is shrouded in that condition and buried. It is said in the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif that no hair is to be shaved from the dead and no nail is to be trimmed.

Our master and lord Jafar, son of our master Sulayman, answered questions put to him by his servant, the author of this book, replying from the island of Yemen to the island of Hind. Among what I asked, I said: what do you say concerning a woman who dies? Is she wrapped in an إزار (izar) and washed as a man is wrapped, or is the end of her wrapper drawn behind her over her private parts and between her thighs until the other end comes round behind her, in the fashion used by the unbelievers and by others among the Muslims? For the Daudi group uses this and denounces whoever does not use it. Is that to be used when she is washed, or not? And is her wrapper to be so arranged in her shrouding, or not? For the Daudi group for the most part uses it in shrouding. They likewise use a ستارة (sitarah) when the dead is washed, screening the body from the women. Is nothing else permitted, or is there no harm in her being washed without a screen over her when she is at a distance from men?

The answer to that: nothing is mentioned in the book of the Pillars except that an إِزَار is placed upon the dead when he is washed, reaching from the navel to the knees, and the water is passed beneath it, and the washer wraps a cloth upon his hand and brings it in under the إِزَار and washes the private parts and the rest of the 'awrah that lies beneath the إِزَار. Practice rests upon that, and the manner you have described prevents its being done. The shrouding is likewise, and concerning it there has come in the book *The Pillars of Islam*, from Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع), that he said:

> نِعْمَ الْكَفَنُ ثَلَاثَةُ أَثْوَابٍ قَمِيصٌ غَيْرُ مَزْرُورٍ وَلَا مَكْفُوفٍ وَلِفَافَةٌ وَاِزَارٌ

The best shroud is three garments: a shirt neither buttoned nor hemmed, a wrapping sheet, and a waist wrapper. Know that. As for the matter of the screen in the washing of the dead — and above all of a woman — the better course is that it be done only within a covering.

And of what I asked, I said: what do you say concerning the meaning of the words of our master al-Qadi al-Numan ibn Muhammad in the Book of Purity, at the end of it, in the mention of the washing of the dead, where he says that the woman is bound up and is given the 'ajrah? What is the meaning of his word وتعجر? The answer to that: the 'ajrah (عجرة) known in the lands of the Arabs, spelled with the undotted راء (ra'), is the gathering of the shirt, drawing together that part of it which faces the navel down to below the navel over the clothing, and tucking it into the fastening of the إِزَار. That is a mark of difference between men and women, like the head covering which is a mark of difference between men and women. Know that.

Our lord the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), said in his Four Hundred Counsels:

> مَنْ مَسَّ جَسَدَ الْمَيِّتِ بَعْدَ مَا بَرَدَ فَعَلَيْهِ الْغُسْلُ

Whoever touches the body of the dead after it has grown cold must perform the washing.

And he said in it:

> مَنْ غَسَّلَ مَيِّتًا فَلْيَغْتَسِلْ بَعْدَ مَا يُلْبِسُهُ الْكَفَنَ وَلَا يَمَسَّهُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَيَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الْغُسْلُ
>
> "Whoever washes a dead person should bathe after he has put the shroud on him; and he must not touch him after that, for then bathing becomes obligatory upon him."

In the book of questions and answers already mentioned, I find this saying explained. Question: what do you say concerning the meaning of the words of the Commander of the Faithful (ع) — that whoever touches the body of the dead after it grows cold is bound to perform the washing? What is the meaning of "after it grows cold"? Answer: it means after his end has come upon him and he has been washed according to the sunnah by whoever washes him, because the body of the dead has become impure; when its moisture reaches a living man it renders him impure, and that is the meaning of the washing being binding upon him.

In the book of questions sent by certain dignitaries of Hind, answered by certain of our lords the summoners in the Yemeni peninsula, I find it written: you asked about a woman who gave birth to two children joined to one another — what is to be done with them, and if one of them dies, what is to be done with him. God, mighty and exalted, creates what He wills. If their adhesion is such that separation is possible, what lies between them is cut without harm to them and without danger, when the matter is slight; but if it is grave and dangerous, they are left as they are. In that case their death is one death and their life is one life, and God knows best, and He does what He wills. If one of them dies and not the other, whatever adheres to the living one is cut from the dead one, as long as the living one feels no sensation or pain from the cutting, if that is possible; the dead one is buried and the living one is left. But if pain is felt in the body of the other, then their life is but one life and their death but one death, and God knows best.

As for the hanut and the shroud, I find it asked in the same book: what do you say concerning what comes in the Book of Reports — that the first thing taken from the estate of the dead is the shroud and his outfitting, then the debt, then the bequest? O our master, if the debt is greater than his estate, is his outfitting to be taken from it according to his station, even if it is costly? Answer: his shroud and his outfitting must be taken out according to his station.

From another place: the hanut is placed upon the places of prostration of the dead, and upon the private parts and the feet, and between the thumb and the forefinger, and upon the navel, the armpits, the breast, the mouth, the eyes, the nose, the forehead, the ears, and the hands at the palms, and the knees. A little oil, wheat, and perfume are put into the water on the third night, and the water is poured upon the grave on the third day. If the dead man is of the people of rank, the Quran is recited over his grave for seven days, and over the graves of others for three days; such has been the practice of our lords, may God lengthen their lives. It has come from our master Hasan ibn Idris that the Quran is recited for the people of rank seven times and for others three times, whether in the mosque, at the graves, in the house, or elsewhere.

In the Mukhtasar al-Athar, I find that the hanut is whatever is of perfume, but neither wars nor saffron is put into the hanut of men, while these are put into the hanut of women. In the Book of Purity, I find that the hanut and the camphor are placed upon the forehead and the nose, the insides of the palms, the knees, and the tops of the feet — these being the places of prostration. From the same book: cotton is placed upon the face, under the armpits, and between the knees, the shins, and the feet, if it is to be had.

In the Tawil al-Daaim, I find that the sunnah concerning the incensing of the dead is this: the dead man himself is not incensed, nor is his bier followed with incense; rather his shroud is incensed, and the place in which he is washed and shrouded — and nothing beyond that. And our lord the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), said in his Four Hundred Counsels:

> وَلَا تُجَمِّرُوا مَوْتَاكُمْ وَلَا تَمَسُّوهُمْ بِالطِّيبِ اِلَّا بِالْكَافُورِ فَاِنَّ الْمَيِّتَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْمُحْرِمِ

Do not perfume your dead with incense, and do not touch them with any fragrance except camphor, for the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage.

In a book of legal questions, all of them remarkable, I find another question: what do you say concerning a man who died, whose head and face were not covered and to whom nothing of the hanut was brought near when he died and was shrouded? Answer: that man died as a pilgrim in a state of consecration, so his head and his face are not covered, and nothing of perfume is brought near him, because he is consecrated during days that are numbered.

As for walking with the bier, I find it asked in the same book: what do you say concerning what comes in the law commanding that one walk behind the bier? O our master, does a man sin if he walks before it, or not? Answer: it is mentioned in the Book of Reports that walking is disliked only before the bier of an enemy of the family, because of the angels of wrath that come to it. As for the believers, it matters not where you walk in relation to the bier, since the angels of mercy encompass it. Yet walking behind it is the more excellent. I find it stated in the Book of Reports that they disliked the call to prayer at the bier, and permitted the informing of people of the death without a public call.

In the Tawil al-Daaim, I find that what is required is this: no one should rise for the bier when it passes except one who intends to follow it, and he should not sit down until it has been set at the edge of the grave. From the Mukhtasar al-Athar: when the dead is brought to the burial ground, the bier is set down crosswise, the dead lying upon his back upon it, so that his right side is toward the qibla and his left toward the one who prays.

From the Tawil al-Daaim, and of that is what is related of the Messenger of God (ع):

> نَظَرَ إِلَى النِّسَاءِ يَتْبَعْنَ جَنَازَةً فَوَقَفَ وَقَالَ لَهُنَّ تُصَلِّينَ عَلَيْهَا فِي مَنْ يُصَلِّي قُلْنَ لَا قَالَ فَتَحْمِلْنَهَا فِي مَنْ يَحْمِلُهَا قُلْنَ لَا قَالَ فَتَنْزِلْنَ لَهَا فِي الْقَبْرِ فِي مَنْ يَنْزِلُهَا قُلْنَ لَا قَالَ فَتُوَارِينَهَا فِي مَنْ يُوَارِيهَا قُلْنَ لَا قَالَ فَارْجِعْنَ مَعْذُورَاتٍ غَيْرَ مَأْجُورَاتٍ
>
> "He saw women following a funeral, and he stopped and said to them: Will you pray over it among those who pray? They said no. Will you carry it among those who carry it? No. Will you go down into the grave among those who go down? No. Will you cover it among those who cover it? No. He said: Then go back, excused but unrewarded."

The *Mukhtasar al-Athar* records that we have transmitted from the Imams of the household of the Messenger of God (ع) that they commanded the following: once the deceased has been shrouded, he is placed upon his bier and laid upon it, when a bier is to be had and this is possible; men carry him on their shoulders, when men can be found. If that is not possible, he is carried on a beast or by whatever other means are available. His shroud is covered from above with a cloth, if one is to be had. A canopy is erected over the bier and it is screened with a cloth; and the deceased is secured if there is fear he may fall from the bier.

On the prayer over the dead, the same book was asked: What do you say concerning a man who dies in a place where no authorized man is present, though an authorized woman is? May she lead the women in the funeral prayer, or should the men pray over him individually and he then be buried? Answer: The prayer of a man is more in keeping with the teaching of the People of the House (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ).

Question: What of the prayer over the dead — is it permitted to pray over him after he has been carried from the place where he was prepared, or not until he reaches the burial ground? Answer: He may be prayed over wherever one wishes: in the burial ground, in his house, or anywhere else. Whoever wishes may recite the supplication between the takbirs of the funeral prayer; whoever wishes may leave it and be content with the imam. The funeral prayer is also permitted during the disliked hours and at the time of an eclipse.

The *Majalis al-Bayan* states that the funeral prayer is a communal obligation upon every Muslim who knows of it, until one of them has performed it, after which the rest participate as volunteers. The Reports record, on the authority of transmitters from the People of the House (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), that it is recommended to pray over the bier within the appointed prayer times, provided there is no risk of missing the prescribed prayer; if that risk exists, one begins with the prescribed prayer.

The *Tawil al-Daaim* likewise states: when the imam of the age is absent, whoever has been appointed judge by him, or given charge by him of some affair of the Muslims, has the better right to the prayer over the dead. If a company of those brought near by the imam's command is present, or of those whom the imam has advanced, the right belongs to the highest among them in station; if only one such person is present, he has a better right to the prayer than the deceased's guardian, being someone the imam has set up, or set up for some affair of the Muslims. Whoever is appointed to lead the people in prayer, if he is present at the bier, has the better right to pray over it. If none of these persons is present, then the most entitled of the guardians has the best right to pray over it.

The *Mukhtasar al-Athar* further states that the funeral prayer is offered over the martyr, over those who have committed grave sins and offenses, and over one killed in execution of a prescribed punishment or in retaliation. The *Mukhtasar* of al-Musannif adds that the supplication is recited quietly during a daytime funeral prayer and aloud during a nighttime one, and that the prayer is offered over one who has taken his own life. From the same book: the deceased's knots are loosened, his right hand is brought out from beneath his side, and his cheek is laid against the earth. If a woman dies carrying a child of six months or more in her womb, the child is taken out if that is possible.

Our master and lord Jafar ibn Sulayman — in his answers to questions put to him by his servant, the author of this book, replying from the island of Yemen to the island of Hind — answered what I asked when I said: What do you say concerning a bier at which one is present, when the imam has come forward to pray over it? Is his recitation of the supplication in the prayer sufficient, or ought the one who follows him to recite it himself as well, given that it is by day? The answer to that: it has come in the book of legal questions and answers that whoever wishes may recite the supplication between the takbirs of the funeral prayer, and whoever wishes may leave it and be content with the imam's recitation. Know that.

As for burial and the graves, it was asked in the same book: What do you say concerning what the law stipulates — that whatever falls from a man while he is alive is to be buried in the earth? O our master, may he bury it wherever he wishes, or only in the burial ground? And if he leaves it and does not bury it, does he sin in that or not? Answer: He buries it wherever he wishes, and there is no blame upon him if it is lost.

Question: What do you say concerning a man in whose land people have buried their dead without his leave, and who, when he came to know of it, wished to have them removed? Is that permitted to him or not? Answer: It is not permitted that burial be made in his land except with his leave; but since they did that without his consent, he has nothing but the value of the places of the graves, and it is not permitted to him to have them removed.

Question: What do you say concerning what the law commands — the burial of the dead where they fell and the prohibition of moving them? O our master, if the burial ground is far off, how is one to act? Answer: The deceased is buried in the place where he dies, in the burial ground of the people of that town, and he is not to be carried to another town. But if he dies in open wilderness, there is no harm in his being carried to the nearest burial ground.

Question: What do you say concerning a woman who dies when there is not to be found in the town any male relative who may lawfully look upon her? Who shall lower her into the grave? Answer: If a woman dies and no kinsman to whom looking upon her is lawful is present at her grave, then the person nearest to her undertakes the burial; and if such a one is lacking, upright men other than her kin bury her out of necessity.

Question: What do you say concerning what comes in the books of the rightly guiding summons — that mud bricks, wood, or whatever else one wishes are placed over the dead, and that if earth is heaped over him it is well? O our master, is it permitted to place over him baked brick, stone, and whatever else is to be found? For the people of the outward sense dislike baked brick. How does the matter stand — may God make us your ransom? Answer: It is permitted to place over him baked brick and whatever else is to be found. Rely upon this and pay no regard to anything else, save what may be done for prudent concealment.

And our lord the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), said in his Four Hundred Counsels:

> أَلِمُّوا بِالْقُبُورِ الَّتِي يَلْزَمُكُمْ حَقُّ سُكَّانِهَا وَزُورُوهَا وَاطْلُبُوا الرِّزْقَ عِنْدَهَا فَأِنَّهُمْ يَفْرَحُونَ بِزِيَارَتِكُمْ وَلْيَطْلُبِ الرَّجُلُ الْحَاجَةَ عِنْدَ قَبْرِ أَبِيهِ وَأُمِّهِ بَعْدَ مَا يَدْعُو لَهُمَا

Visit the graves of those who have a claim upon you. Go to them, and seek provision at their graves, for they rejoice at your visiting. Let a man ask for what he needs at the grave of his father and his mother, after he has prayed for them both.

edits.chapter_key: the charity of the head
edits.body_md:
I turn now to the zakat of Fitr.

In the first book of questions and answers — arranged according to the chapter order of the Book of the Pillars of Islam — the following exchange appears. Question: the custom among the Indians when collecting the fitra is to mix four kinds of grain — rice, maize, wheat, and salt — and then take their monetary value, whereas in the radiant Shariah the zakat of Fitr is a sa of dates, raisins, wheat, or barley. Does it suffice a person who gives a sa of barley? Answer: the reliance is on what is stated in the Pillars — that is, a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins.

> وَالْفِطْرَةُ مِنْ أَطْيَبِ مَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَأَزْكَى مَا تَدَّخِرُونَ

The fitra is to be from the best of what you eat and the purest of what you store away.

Whoever mixes the fitra from everything he ate during Ramadan, that suffices him; and whoever ate nothing but barley, that too suffices him. Verify this well.

Question: what is the ruling for a man who wishes to pay his fitra before Ramadan begins, fearing that poverty or travel may prevent him from paying it at its proper time? What does the noble law say on this — does it suffice him or not? The question arises because obligatory duties may not be performed outside their appointed times, nor made up except after those times have passed. And if it does not suffice him, it should be noted that the Book of the Pillars states there is no harm in collecting zakat from those who owe it before its due time, when there is need for that. Please provide the answer on this, and also address the case of one who did this out of ignorance — has it sufficed him? Answer: if he delivers his fitra to someone who has the right to receive it, it has sufficed him. The prohibition in this matter is that a person should not break his fast before delivering his fitra. No fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it; the obligation is simply its delivery.

He stated in the book Mukhtasar al-Musannaf: a dhimmi who accepts Islam before the break of dawn on the day of Fitr owes the zakat of Fitr; if he accepts Islam after the break of dawn, nothing is due from him.

He stated in the reports: they narrated that the zakat of Fitr is paid on behalf of the mukatab. He stated in the Landmarks of Religion: if a child is born before the break of dawn on the day of Fitr, the zakat of Fitr is due on his behalf. He stated in the Book of the Pillars: it has likewise been said that it is paid on behalf of the child still in his mother's womb, before birth. He stated in the Selected Book: or a sa of dried curd, or half a sa of wheat. He stated in the Landmarks of Religion that the weight of the sa is four and a half ratls by the ratl of Mecca; he stated therein that its weight by the ratl of Medina is five ratls less a third of a ratl; and its weight by the Baghdadi ratl is nine ratls and a tenth of a ratl.

Our master and lord, the author of the Mustansiriyya sessions — peace of God be upon him — stated in the thirteenth session: since we mentioned in the session before this one the zakat that is obligatory upon those who possess wealth, we follow that with the mention of the zakat that is obligatory in every condition, and upon those of small means who give it in charity — and that is the zakat of Fitr. In it are seven obligations and twelve practices of the Sunnah. The obligations are:

1. that a man pay it on behalf of himself;
2. on behalf of the elder of his household;
3. and the younger of them;
4. and the free among them;
5. and the enslaved among them;
6. and the males among them;
7. and the females among them.

The practices of the Sunnah are that he bring it out from the middle sort of what he eats — a sa of wheat, or a sa of barley, or a sa of dates, or a sa of raisins; half a sa of wheat suffices him, and from anything other than wheat nothing suffices but a full sa; and the sa is four mudds. He should hand it to the Imam (ع), or to whomever the Imam has appointed; it should be brought out before the breaking of the fast; whoever delays bringing it out must make it up; and whoever lacks the food brings out its value in silver or in gold. As for the woman who has no husband with her, she brings it out on behalf of herself and on behalf of those she supports.

He stated in the book of the Inner Nursing, regarding the saying of the Messenger of God:

> اَلْفِطْرَةُ لَا تَحِلُّ لِي وَلَا لِأَهْلِ بَيْتِي

The fitra is not lawful for me, nor for the people of my house.

Our master Zayd ibn Muhammad — may God sanctify his spirit — stated in the Concealed Epistle: as for the charity of Fitr, the Messenger of God made it obligatory upon every head among the Muslims to pay his fitra — upon the males and the females, the small and the great, even the infant born on that very day — and it is paid on behalf of the child in his mother's womb. He made obligatory upon every head a sa of wheat, dates, raisins, barley, or other grains. He stated therein:

> وَسُمِّيَتْ صَدَقَةُ الْفِطْرِ صَدَقَةَ الرَّأْسِ

The charity of Fitr has been named the charity of the head.

He stated therein: it is paid before the prayer, and if it is paid before the prayer it is charity. He stated therein: if the child is born after the Fitr, the fitra is paid before the Fitr.

He stated in the book Mafatih al-Nima — which belongs to our master the Judge al-Numan ibn Muhammad, may God exalt his sanctity — concerning the fitra:

> فَاِنْ أُخْرِجَتْ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ كَانَتْ فِطْرَةً وَإِذَا أُخْرِجَتْ بَعْدَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ كَانَتْ صَدَقَةً

If it is brought out before sunrise, it counts as fitra; if it is brought out after sunrise, it is ordinary charity.

He stated, up to his words:

> وَمَعْنَى الْفِطْرَةِ إِخْرَاجُ الْوَاجِبِ لِلَّهِ وَلِوَلِيِّهِ مِنَ الْفِكَاكِ وَالْقُرْبَانِ

The meaning of fitra is the bringing out of what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and as offering.

I turn now to various rulings on zakat, on the one upon whom no zakat falls, and on other matters. In a book of legal questions — each one a marvel — he raised another question: what do you say concerning a man for whom the zakat on his wealth has been made lawful? The answer: in that case he is a man who owns a thousand dinars and owes a thousand dinars, so there is no zakat upon him on it. He stated therein another question: what do you say concerning a man for whom the zakat on his wealth is lawful while he himself is well off? The answer: in that case he is a man among the polytheists who has found no Muslim to whom to hand the zakat of his wealth, so he has more right to it than anyone else.

edits.chapter_key: the sun, the moon, and the order of obedience
edits.body_md:
It is the nobler of the two, and the more fitting to be relied upon in the performance of obligatory duties. In saying this, we have not set aside the ruling of the sighting of the eye (رُؤْيَةُ الْعَيْنِ), for these two sightings are both foundations in the performance of obligatory duties — one simply more excellent than the other. The more excellent belongs to the select, those who go before others by their knowledge: they are the possessors of knowledge (أُولُوا الْعِلْم). The other belongs to the generality, whose ignorance obliges them to follow the people of knowledge — those who are bare of understanding. The relation between the two sightings is like the relation between the two times of a prayer, the first of which is more excellent than the second.

So it is with all matters: they come in two kinds, hidden and apparent. The hidden is known only by the select among the excellent, while the apparent is known by both the select and the generality alike. The select are obliged to carry out what follows from what they have come to know, just as the common people are obliged to carry out what follows from what they have come to know. This being so, what is there to deny in the following: that a learned man, by the excellence of his knowledge, is bound to fast by the hidden vision of the soul (الرُّؤْيَةُ النَّفْسَانِيَّةُ), and that an ignorant man is bound to follow the learned man in that? It is precisely as with the one taking the pre-dawn meal who knows, by his hidden knowledge, that dawn has broken — for whom food, drink, and marital relations become forbidden, and fasting becomes binding — while the one taking the pre-dawn meal who is ignorant of the dawn must follow the learned man in that.

As for the saying of the Prophet (ع),

> فَإِنْ غُمَّ عَلَيْكُمْ فَعُدُّوا ثَلَاثِينَ يَوْماً

"If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days" — upon consideration, it can scarcely be held that what he intended by it was the sighting of the eye. For fasting by the sight of the eye, when the impediments of cloud and the like are lifted, can hardly ever yield months of thirty days; a month may well be twenty-nine days. And if that is so, it is not permissible that the Prophet (ع) should bind his community, in one of the commands of Allah Almighty, to a rule in which doubt may arise — making this the cause of an addition to an obligation or a subtraction from it, and leaving his community to perform it as though walking in the dark. Nor is it permissible that he should command his community to fast an added day in one of the deficient months on account of cloud, when, had the cloud not been there, it would have been known that fasting on that day is forbidden and that breaking the fast is required. For fasting is worship of Allah Almighty, and it belongs to the religion by which Allah is served; His servants are commanded to sincerity in it, by the saying of Allah Almighty:

> وَمَآ أُمِرُوٓا۟ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ
>
> "They were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion."

Sincerity is other than doubt and confusion. And since sincerity is other than doubt and confusion, and since doubt and confusion have entered into this rule and disturbed it, we say that the Prophet (ع) did not call people to doubt and confusion in the worship of Allah Almighty. And since the Prophet (ع) did not call to doubt and confusion, his restricting the days of the month to the fullest and most complete number — without deficiency and without the lesser count — when by the requirement of the sight of the eye the days of a month may be deficient and doubt may fall upon it, can only have been an indication pointing toward the vision of the soul, whose numbers neither increase nor decrease. It was an urging to take hold of what Allah Almighty called for in the completing of the count, in His saying:

> وَلِتُكْمِلُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ
>
> "And that you may complete the count."

Then we say: from where comes the assurance of a people whose fast, when cloud and impediment occur, rests upon that rule — the assurance that the day they counted as belonging to Ramadan or to Shaban, under a clouded sky, is indeed as they counted and reckoned it, when that very same day, for another people of their own school in taking the sight of the eye, is otherwise, because the impediments of cloud and the like have been lifted for them? So, for example, there is cloud in Kirman, and their fast differs from the fast of Shiraz, where, say, there is no cloud. And if it were permissible for the time of the fast to differ among the people of a single region — so that fasting becomes obligatory upon one people on a given day and upon another people on the following day — then it would likewise be permissible for the time of prayer to differ among the people of a single town, so that one and the same prayer becomes binding upon one man at one time and upon another man at another time. Since that is not permissible, and since, when the time of a prayer has come, the community is bound to establish it whether a man establishes it or abandons it, so likewise, when the time of the fast has come, the fast is binding upon the community, whether a man fasts or breaks it.

This being so, the saying of the Prophet (ع) is an indication given by him — knowing that error may fall in the sighting of the eye — pointing to that in which error does not fall: namely, the vision of the soul, which is knowledge, and its count, which belongs among the matters he commended, that is, the completing of the count. Further, his saying, "If it is obscured from you, then count thirty," requires, for entering the fast, that the counting be from the days of Shaban, and, for leaving it by breaking the fast, that the counting be from the days of Ramadan. Now it is known that counting is not possible except by having something to count and knowing its first day. It is also known that in most cases the crescent is not seen at the beginnings of the months, on account of impediments that prevent the sight from seeing it — especially in places whose air is turbid, such as Tabaristan, the mountain regions, the coasts, and the islands of the sea. And if it is possible that the crescent is not seen by the eye at the beginning of Shaban, and is not seen because of some obstacle that occurs, and its first day is not known, then how is one to count from it? And how is one to count from Ramadan when its first day has not been verified? To carry this report upon the meaning of the sighting of the eye requires that the Prophet (ع) cast his community into disagreement and called them to what lies beyond their capacity — namely, the counting of the days of a month whose beginning is not known and in which the crescent is not seen. Yet Allah Almighty says:

> لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
>
> "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity."

Since such a thing cannot be imagined of the Prophet (ع) — who stands far removed and sanctified above burdening Allah's servants with what lies beyond them or casting them into disagreement — it must follow that either the report "If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days" is not sound, or that if the Prophet (ع) did say it, it must be taken in the one sense that is sound and that removes what is objectionable, and in no other sense. And since this is necessary, and the testimonies have established that what is sound — and what creation is called to — is the vision of the soul, which is knowledge, we say: the discussion has now made clear that what is intended is other than the sighting of the eye, that the common people, who are limited in knowledge, are bound to follow, and that the objection raised in this matter has been overturned.

Then we say: which of the pillars of Islam that Muhammad (ع) brought has ever had its affair entrusted to the community — a community that is not preserved from error and that falls into slip and mistake? Prayer? Fasting? Zakat? Hajj? Jihad? That fasting alone should forever be committed to them, in the seeking of the crescent and the knowing of its times? Is not prayer the pillar of religion and the face of Islam, and are not all its acts — the opening takbir, the recitation, the bowing, the prostration, and the salutation — committed to the Imam who stands in the place of the Messenger (ع) in leading the people in prayer, and not to those who follow him? Upon those who follow lies the following of the Imam in these acts, without their own preference being followed in advancing any of its acts or in delaying any of its limits; and whoever among them does this — advancing or delaying — his prayer is deficient (خِدَاج). Is not the collecting of zakat committed to the Imam who stands in the place of the Messenger (ع), so that setting it aside or turning it away from him is not permissible, and the distributing of what comes of it belongs to him among those who respond to him, and not to the community, as it was in the days of the Prophet (ع)? Whoever gives his zakat to one other than him who stands in the place of the Messenger (ع) must render it a second time, just as one who, in the days of the Prophet (ع), gave his zakat to another than him would have been bound to render it to him a second time, because he placed it where it did not belong. Is not the Hajj incomplete except with the Imam who goes before the assembly, so that they are bound to follow him in the rites he performs, and whoever sets himself apart by advancing one rite before another or by delaying it, his Hajj is deficient? Is not the ordering of jihad in the way of Allah committed to the one entrusted with the affair of the Muslims who fight — in preserving their order and all their condition, in leading them forward in battle and in withdrawal, and in seeking what is best in truce and in fighting? Upon the community that fights lies the following of the one who commands among them by the command of Allah, and not the following of their own desires in peace and in war; and whoever does anything of that fighting without his command and sheds blood without his permission is held answerable for it.

This being so, and the foundations of Islam being committed to one who preserves them, the community being obliged to follow him in them, from where has it become permissible for these people to follow their own opinions in the entering of the fast — which is one of those foundations — without following in it the one who stands in the place of the Messenger (ع)? Is this severance of theirs, this entering of the fast by their own ijtihad — which brings them to make obligatory what is not an obligation, to abandon an obligation, or to count it a Sunnah — anything other than presumption against Allah, or a departure from the safeguarding of His command? We seek refuge in Allah from that.

If he says: "On the principle you have laid down for the entering of the fast, namely conjunction and separation, the day on which conjunction and separation fall must be partly of Shaban and partly of Ramadan, and the fasting of that part becomes binding; and this is a contradiction, which the Prophet (ع) did not command," we say: the Prophet (ع) imposed the obligations on behalf of Allah, and appointed for each obligation two causes by which it becomes due and binding. The first is a preceding cause, by which the second cause is made valid; the second is the cause by which one obligation is distinguished from another. The first is general — it is a cause for this obligation and for others besides it, so that in performing the obligation one does not take hold of it alone but of the second. The second follows upon the general one and is specific — it belongs to that obligation alone, and by it the obligation is set apart from all else.

- **Prayer:** Since this prayer is not obligatory except by day, the day is its preceding general cause — a cause for this prayer and for the other prayers performed by day alike. Then, since this prayer is not obligatory by the mere occurrence of that preceding cause, which is the day, except when the sun declines from the zenith, the declining of the sun is a second cause by which the prayer becomes obligatory and by which one takes hold in performing it; and it is specific.

- **Zakat:** Since zakat is not obligatory except upon wealth, wealth is the cause of the obligation of zakat, and it is a preceding general cause. Then, since zakat is not obligatory by the mere occurrence of that preceding cause, which is wealth, except when a year has passed over it, the year is a second cause by which it becomes due and by which one takes hold in performing it; and it is specific.

- **Hajj:** Since the Hajj is not obligatory except with ability, ability is its preceding general cause. Then, since a man does not become obligated to perform the Hajj by the mere occurrence of ability — the preceding cause — except on the greatest day at Mecca, that day is a second cause by which one takes hold in fulfilling it; and it is specific.

- **Jihad:** Since jihad is not obligatory except with the occurrence of opposition, the raising of the standard of disobedience, and the refusal of obedience, opposition is the preceding general cause. Then, since jihad is not obligatory by the mere existence of opposition and refusal of obedience except through the standing of the one who holds the place of the Messenger (ع) and a head who leads the community into battle, that is a second cause; and it is specific.

Since that is so, we say that fasting too has two causes. The first is preceding and general: the separation of the moon from the sun. The second is specific: the time of dawn at which entering into the fast becomes obligatory. And just as prayer is not obligatory — though it be day — except at the declining of the sun, and that is its time; nor zakat — though there be wealth — except when a year has passed over it, and that is its time; nor Hajj — though there be ability — except at Mecca on the greatest day, and that is its time; nor jihad — though there be opposition — except through the ordering head who stands in the place of the Lord of the worlds, and he is its support; so likewise fasting is not obligatory — though the moon has separated from the sun — except at the dawn that follows upon that separation, and that is its time. His saying in objection — that part of the day is of Shaban and part of it is of Ramadan and that the fasting of that part is consequently binding — is thus overturned.

What adds to the certainty of this, along with the proofs already established from the apparent, is the greatest testimony, which speaks to the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ع) in what he brought from Allah Almighty: the balance between what he laid down of the Law and the religious ordinances and what Allah Almighty created and formed in the horizons and in the souls, as stated in the saying of Allah:

> سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ
>
> "We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and in their own souls, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth."

No human being has the power to imitate him in such a work, save one whose lineage is in the holy precinct (حَظِيرَةُ الْقُدْسِ) and whose soul has been given readiness and endowment for receiving the revelation of Allah Almighty, when one returns to the interpretation, which is one of the two divisions to which Allah commanded His Prophet (ع) to call His servants in His worship, in His saying:

> ٱدْعُ إِلَىٰ سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِٱلْحِكْمَةِ
>
> "Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom."

This wisdom has two divisions:

- The work: the outward, natural worship suited to natural bodies, carried out through the obligations and practices the Prophet (ع) brought, and requiring interpretation — that is, knowledge.
- The knowledge: the greatest form of worship, the hidden worship of the soul, suited to particular souls. It is attained by holding to the truths concerning how to purify the affirmation of Allah's oneness, and by so doing it confirms the outward natural worship, which is the work.

In the interpretive call, the sun — in that it is the noblest and most luminous of bodies, the source of light for all others, the cause of growth among offspring in the world of nature, and the cause to which all the causes of the world are attached — has been made an indication pointing to knowledge of the rank of the Prophet (ع). Just as the sun is the noblest and most luminous of bodies, so the soul of the Speaker is the noblest of souls and the most knowing of them. Just as the sun is the source of light for the other stars, so the soul of the Speaker (ع) is the source for the souls of men in the divine sciences that lead to the pure affirmation of oneness. Just as the sun is the cause of growth among offspring in the world of nature, so the Prophet (ع) is the cause of growth among spiritual offspring in the world of the soul. And just as the sun is the cause to which the causes of the bodily world are attached, so the Prophet (ع) is the cause to which the causes of the world of religion are attached, which is the worship of Allah Almighty. The one is in the body, and the other is in the soul.

As for the moon: its rank falls below the sun; it receives more of the sun's light than the other stars receive; it gives light in the darkness of the night; and it stands as an intermediary in the growth of offspring between the earth and the sun, both receiving and bestowing. For these reasons, the moon has been made an indication pointing to the rank of the Foundation (الْأَسَاس). Just as the moon's rank in light falls below the sun, so the rank of the Foundation in receiving the radiance of the world of origination falls below the Prophet (ع).

I have said that the moon receives more of the sun's light than any other of the wandering bodies; and in just the same way, the Foundation (الْأَسَاس) receives from the Speaker (اَلنَّاطِق) more of the blessings of the affirmation of Allah's oneness than any other recipient does. Just as the moon gives light in the darkness of the night, so the Foundation makes plain what the Prophet (ع) brought of the sealed symbols, the law set out in its breadth, and the parables that were struck. And just as the moon is the intermediary between the sun and the other bodies in the growth of offspring, so the Foundation is the intermediary between the Speaker and the community in the growth of spiritual offspring in the world of the soul, both conferring benefit and receiving it.

Now that the states of the bodily sun and moon in the world of bodies have been set beside the states of the spiritual sun and moon in the world of religion, I say that the moon has several states:

- When it comes into conjunction with the sun, the upper half of its body — the half that faces the sun — is illumined. This is what the astronomers mean when they say that a power extends to it, by which everything that is to come into being of events and existing things is brought into being until the second conjunction, by a measure ordained from the Mighty, the All-Knowing. It is like a minister who comes into the presence of the king: the king charges him concerning the affairs of the kingdom with what he is to carry out once he has left the royal presence. So it is with the Prophet (ع) teaching the Foundation (ع) what he wished to teach him, that he might stand in the Prophet's place in guidance and instruction — the Foundation receiving from him in his days, conferring nothing before that designation. It is for this reason that the Prophet (ع) pointed to Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع) and said:

> "أَنَا مَدِينَةُ الْعِلْمِ وَعَلِيٌّ بَابُهَا فَمَنْ أَرَادَ الْعِلْمَ فَلْيَأْتِ الْبَابَ"
>
> "I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate. Whoever desires knowledge, let him come to the gate."

- After the parting, the moon falls into hiddenness, lying beneath the light of the sun, concealed from the sight of the generality of people and seen only by those possessed of knowledge. This is like the hiddenness of the affair of the Foundation — his rank and the obligation of obedience to him, established by means of the indications made toward him — hidden from the people of ignorance and from the common people, and disclosed only to those of merit and special standing.

- When the sun has reached its setting place, the moon appears as a crescent so that the great and the small alike behold it. This is like the manifestation of the Foundation's affair through what came from the Speaker (ع) in the explicit text concerning him and the imposing of obedience to him, when the time of his own departure from the world drew near, so that the small and the great came to know it.

- The moon has no light during the day while the disc of the sun stands above the earth, and has light only after the sun has set. This is like the Foundation, who has no affair during the lifetime of the Speaker (ع), and only after his departure from the world.

- At the beginning of its appearance it is faint, seen only by one whose sight is strong, and people fall into disagreement over the sighting of it. This is like the weakness of the affair of the Foundation at the beginning of its season, the arising of disagreement concerning his Imamate, and the shrinking back of the community from binding themselves to obedience to him, except for one who possessed sincerity and knowledge.

- Its light increases with the passing of the days. So too the affair of his summons rises and his Imamate spreads among the people with the passing of the years.

- When fourteen days of it have passed, its light is complete, so that the small and the great see it and no one doubts the sighting of it. This is like the light of his Imamate reaching all the nations at the passing of the seven repetitions (اَلْمَثَانِي السَّبْعَةُ) at the end of the cycle, so that at that time no one doubts his Imamate and his precedence.

Then there is the fact that the people of knowledge and faith assign the day that falls within the concealment after the parting to the coming month — just as one of sound faith held himself bound, by what he knew of the indications of the Prophet (ع) given to a few in particular, to obedience to the Commander of the Faithful before the explicit text was given outwardly for all. The people of ignorance and the common people, by contrast, assign that day — whose fast is obligatory — to the month now past, whose fast is not obligatory, through the scantness of their knowledge, and so they fail in fasting it until they see the crescent with the eye. In the same way, they assign to the Foundation — obedience to whom is obligatory — the same standing as any other to whom obedience is not made obligatory, neither by indication nor by explicit text, and they fail in obedience to him out of ignorance of its being binding upon them, until the truth of his Imamate becomes plain to them.

The month of Ramadan is, among the months of the year, the noblest of them and the greatest in weight. It stands for the Foundation, who is placed ahead of the rest of the companions, whose rank was ennobled by exposition and interpretation — which is knowledge — who was pointed to by the indications, and who is the gathering place of the knowledge of all that the Prophet (ع) brought from Allah the Exalted. It is for this reason that Allah the Exalted said:

> "شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ فِيهِ الْقُرْآنُ هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ وَالْبَيِّنَاتِ مِنَ الْهُدَى وَالْفُرْقَانِ"
>
> "The month of Ramadan, in which the Quran was sent down as guidance for the people, and as clear proofs of guidance and of the criterion."

This verse was intended as an indication pointing to him. We know, after all, that the Quran was revealed over twenty-three years — not all at once in the month of Ramadan, but day by day, month by month, and year by year. To read this verse according to its outward sense leads directly to contradiction. Interpretation is therefore necessary, so that the word of Allah the Exalted and the word of the Messenger (ع) may each stand firm, together with the binding character of the fast and its obligation upon the sighting of the crescent: first, on the side of the soul, for the people of knowledge, at the very moment of their sighting; and last, on the side of the senses, for the people of ignorance. The same principle governs the obligation of obedience to the Foundation (ع) — when the Prophet (ع) raised him to this station and pointed to him, he did so first through indications understood by those with knowledge and discernment, and last through explicit text and formal declaration for the common people. The same principle also governs the obligation upon whoever is present to hold back from opening discourse and from teaching, even while the Foundation stands ahead of the assembly. It is for this that Allah the Exalted said:

> "لَا تَرْفَعُوٓا۟ أَصْوَتَكُمْ فَوْقَ صَوْتِ ٱلنَّبِىِّ"
>
> "Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet."

This forbids the community from overstepping in a way that would drive out the ruling of Allah the Exalted and narrow it rather than widen it — by going ahead of the Messenger in his time, and ahead of the Foundation and whoever stands in their place in their own time — so that the Imam may be distinguished from those who follow him, and the head from those under him. Then He said:

> "من شهد منكم الشهر فليصمه"
>
> "Whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it."

This is an indication from the Speaker to the community that follows him: they are to follow the Foundation and to listen in silence to his speech. The meaning is that whoever attends the assembly of the Foundation in the knowledge of the outward and the inward, let him keep silent — for it is the Foundation who has been honored, who is placed ahead, and to whom the affair of religion is entrusted, and no one else. This is evidence that before obedience to him was made obligatory, the people used to discourse with one another in matters of religion and knowledge however they wished, and were then forbidden from it — just as before the fast and its obligation they used to eat however they liked, and were then forbidden from it by the imposing of the fast. It is like the command of the Prophet (ع) in the matter of marriage, when he said:

> "لَا نِكَاحَ إِلَّا بِوَلِيٍّ وَشَاهِدَيْنِ"
>
> "There is no marriage except with a guardian and two witnesses."

This shows that marriage had previously been contracted without a guardian or two witnesses — that is, temporary marriage (اَلْمُتْعَة) — however people wished, in the early days of Islam, and that they were then forbidden from this practice by this ruling.

Then His word:

> "وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ فَعِدَّةٌۭ مِّنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ"
>
> "And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days."

This is an exception that applies to all who witness the month. The meaning is that silence has been made obligatory upon all people when they attend the assembly of interpretation ascribed to the Foundation — except for one whose speech is for the sake of receiving benefit: a man in doubt, or a learner. In such a case, silence again becomes binding upon him afterward according to the rule. For attendance at that assembly is the prayer of the soul and of knowledge, and what is required in the prayer of works must equally be observed within it: the etiquettes, the customary practices, and the upholding of the rulings. I have also set down in the comprehensive treatise a portion concerning the fast, with explanation and clarification, to the measure of the benefits that have reached me from the side of the guardian of Allah (ع).

As for the month of Ramadan of the year four hundred — and the agreement of the people of truth to enter its fast two days before the crescent was sighted with the eye — this is a matter that, upon my life, is confusing to all but the people of understanding, given that no more than a single day of difference had ever been known to pass between the fast of the people of truth and the fast of the people of disagreement.

The reason is this: the conjunction that occurred in the month of Ramadan fell on the night of Monday, making Monday its first day. The crescent was not seen on Tuesday night by naked-eye sighting, because the sun's light overpowered its body. At the time of sunset, the moon stood at six degrees and some minutes from the sun — a distance equal to half the moon's body — and at such a distance the sight cannot reach it, since it falls beneath the ray that prevents sight from doing its work. It was therefore not permissible, out of propriety, to break the fast on that day, for the moon stood from the sun at the end of the month at a like number of degrees. Had one broken the fast then, what could have been fasted of the month of Ramadan would have amounted to only twenty-nine days — because the conjunction of the sun and the moon for Shawwal fell on the night of Wednesday, at two hours and some minutes into it, making Wednesday the day of the festival, on which fasting is forbidden. A failure in one of the obligatory duties would thus have occurred, since the month of Ramadan is thirty days without deficiency, by the word of our masters (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ):

> "مَا تَمَّ شَعْبَانُ وَلَا نَقَصَ رَمَضَانُ"

The strongest proof of the soundness of our entering the fast from Monday is the word of the Prophet (ع):

> "يَوْمُ صَوْمِكُمْ يَوْمُ نَحْرِكُمْ"
>
> "The day of your fasting is the day of your sacrifice."

The sacrifice in the Sacred Precinct fell on Monday, the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah of the year four hundred — according to what the sighting by knowledge requires — which is the ninth of it according to what the sighting by the eye requires. And the matter holds in this way every year, as he said (ع), without any disagreement arising.

If someone should say: what you have brought forward concerning the sun and the moon, the degrees, the distances, and the hours, and on which you have built your argument and your proof, belongs to the science of the stars, and the Prophet (ع) forbade taking it up and looking into it — I say: how is it that inference concerning the establishing of the time of the fast, and knowledge of it by way of the sun and the moon, which are the cause of the months and the years and which cannot be attained except through their motion, their course, their conjunction, and their separation, is forbidden to us, while inference concerning the establishing of the direction of prayer and the times of prayer, and the knowledge of them — which is like the fast in being among the pillars of Islam — by way of the mansions of the moon and the elevation of the sun with the measures we have set up for you, is commanded? Is this anything other than an unjust division (قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَى)?

The Prophet (ع) forbade it only in a particular respect. It is that whoever begins the pursuit of the sciences by learning the science of the stars, without the divine and revealed sciences preceding it for him, is led by that path to what the followers of Ptolemy hold, and those who ascribe divinity to the heavenly bodies. But when the religious and revealed sciences have preceded it, then knowledge of the manner of the spheres and the stars, and of that for which they were composed, increases the soul in certainty concerning the oneness of Allah the Exalted, and gains for its conception of His unity a firmer faith. So too Allah the Exalted said:

> "لَخَلْقُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ أَكْبَرُ مِنْ خَلْقِ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ"
>
> "The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most people do not know."

And He said:

> "سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ"
>
> "We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth."

The horizons are nothing other than the heavens and all they contain. Moreover, had the matter been as that objector claimed, Allah the Exalted would not have sworn by the stars, nor would He have described them as indicating His unity in His Book, where He says:

> "تَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ بُرُوجًۭا وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا سِرَجًۭا وَقَمَرًۭا مُّنِيرًۭا"
>
> "Blessed is He who placed constellations in the sky and placed in it a lamp and an illuminating moon."

Nor would He have sworn, saying:

> "فلا أقسم بمواقع النجوم وأنه قسم لو تعلمون عظيم"
>
> "So I swear by the settings of the stars, and it is indeed a great oath, if you only knew."

And He said:

> "فَلَا أُقْسِمُ بِالْخُنَّسِ الْجَوَارِ الْكُنَّسِ"
>
> "So I swear by the receding stars, that run their course and hide."

And He said:

> "فَالْمُدَبِّرَاتِ أَمْرًا"
>
> "And those that arrange the affair."

And He said:

> "وَٱلسَّمَآءِ ذَاتِ ٱلْبُرُوجِ"
>
> "By the sky containing the constellations."

And He said:

> "وَالشَّمْسِ وَضُحَاهَا وَالْقَمَرِ إِذَا تَلَاهَا"

And He said:

> "هُوَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ ٱلشَّمْسَ ضِيَآءًۭ وَٱلْقَمَرَ نُورًۭا وَقَدَّرَهُۥ مَنَازِلَ لِتَعْلَمُوا۟ عَدَدَ ٱلسِّنِينَ وَٱلْحِسَابَ"
>
> "It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stages, that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning."

What merit, then, is nobler than knowledge of the luminous stars in their circles — their positions at their highest and their lowest — which testify to the soundness of what Allah the Exalted has established of His religion, and bear witness to the truth of what the Prophet (ع) brought from Allah? And what knowledge stands higher, after the affirmation of oneness and the ranks of the hudud (الْحُدُود), than knowledge of what arises through the passage of the stars through their constellations — southward and northward — and through the conjunctions of their lights with one another, in the world of generation and corruption, in the appearance of offspring and in other events that point to the ranks of the friends of Allah?

> "فَهَلْ يَسْتَوِي الظُّلُمَاتُ وَالنُّورُ أَمْ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الْأَعْمَى وَالْبَصِيرُ أَمْ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ وَالَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ إِنَّمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ أُولُوا الْأَلْبَابِ"

Are darkness and light equal? Or are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are those who know and those who do not know equal? Only those of understanding take heed.

By the testimonies I have brought forward — outward and inward alike — it is now established that sighting is of two kinds; that choosing the more excellent of the two in fulfilling one's obligatory duties is the better course; and that when the Prophet (ع) used the letter ل (اَللَّام) in his words لرؤيته, he intended by it the sighting of knowledge — which requires that the people already be fasting when the crescent is sighted with the eye, and not otherwise.

Know this, then — and may Allah grant you success in obeying Him and obeying His friends — and take hold of the meanings of what I have set forth. Seek Allah's help in all your affairs, and draw near to Him through sincerity of intention and of inward purpose, both in your worship of Him and in your obedience to His friends, for He is the best helper toward whatever one seeks to know of the realities. And give thanks to Allah the Exalted for every blessing that reaches you from the side of His trustees.

Here I bring the treatise to its close, and I close it as it began — with praise belonging to Allah and with prayers upon those through whom His guidance reaches us. > وَبَعْدُ فَقَدْ خَتَمْتُ الرِّسَالَةَ بِالْحَمْدِ لِلَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْأَعْلَى وَبِالصَّلَاةِ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ مُحَمَّدٍ الْمُصْطَفَى وَالْوَلِيِّ عَلِيٍّ الْمُرْتَضَى وَالْأَئِمَّةِ الطَّاهِرِينَ أَقْمَارِ الدُّجَى

I have sealed this treatise with praise of Allah, the High, the Most High, and with prayer upon the Prophet Muhammad the Chosen, upon the guardian Ali the Well-Pleasing, and upon the pure Imams, the moons amid the darkness.

> وَإِمَامِ الزَّمَانِ مَوْلَانَا وَهَادِينَا وَوَلِيِّ نِعَمِنَا الْإِمَامِ الْحَاكِمِ بِأَمْرِ اللَّهِ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ صَلَوَاتُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَى آبَائِهِ الطَّاهِرِينَ وَأَبْنَائِهِ الْأَكْرَمِينَ الْمُنْتَظَرِينَ إِلَى يَوْمِ الدِّينِ أَفْضَلُ التَّحِيَّاتِ وَالتَّسْلِيمِ

Upon the Imam of the age — our master, our guide, and the guardian of our blessings — the Imam who rules by the command of Allah, the Commander of the Faithful: may Allah's prayers be upon him, upon his pure forefathers, and upon his noble sons who are awaited until the Day of Judgment, the finest of greetings and salutations.

> وَنَسْأَلُ اللَّهَ أَنْ يُثَبِّتَنَا عَلَى طَاعَتِهِ وَطَاعَةِ أَوْلِيَائِهِ وَيُنَوِّرَ عُقُولَنَا وَبَصَائِرَنَا بِمَنِّهِ وَكَرَمِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ إِنَّهُ خَيْرُ مَسْئُولٍ وَأَكْرَمُ مَأْمُولٍ وَحَسْبُنَا اللَّهُ وَنِعْمَ الْوَكِيلُ وَنِعْمَ الْمَوْلَى وَنِعْمَ النَّصِيرُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَى سَيِّدِنَا مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ وَسَلَّمَ

We ask Allah to keep us steadfast in obedience to Him and to His friends, and to illumine our minds and our inner sight through His favor, His generosity, and His power. He is the finest of all who are asked and the most generous of all in whom hope is placed. Allah is our sufficiency — the best of guardians, the best of masters, and the best of helpers. May Allah bless our master Muhammad and his family, and grant them peace.
